blocks.html: In The Magnitude Scale you met the astronomer's way of saying how bright a star looks: smaller numbers are brighter, and 5 magnitudes means a factor of 100 in brightness. That rule came from the naked-eye catalogs of ancient Greece, which sorted stars into six classes. In 1856 Norman Pogson made it exact. Now we turn it into an equation you can solve, using properties of logarithms.
What a magnitude measures is the flux $F$: the power of starlight arriving per square meter of telescope, in W/m², usually through a filter that passes one band of colors.

Suppose one step of 1 magnitude is always the same factor $r$ in flux. Five steps multiply: $r^5 = 100$, so $r = 100^{1/5} = 10^{0.4} \approx 2.512$. A difference of $\Delta m$ magnitudes is then $\Delta m$ steps, a factor of $10^{0.4\,\Delta m}$. Taking $\log_{10}$ turns that power back into a difference: magnitudes are a logarithm of flux, so ratios of fluxes become differences of magnitudes. The minus sign is there because the scale runs backward: more flux, smaller magnitude.
Two stars' magnitudes and fluxes are linked by $$m_1 - m_2 = -2.5\log_{10}\frac{F_1}{F_2}, \qquad \frac{F_1}{F_2} = 10^{-0.4\,(m_1 - m_2)}.$$

blocks.cap: Every 2.5 magnitudes is exactly a factor of 10. That makes quick estimates easy.

blocks.title: From magnitudes to a flux ratio
blocks.q: Vega has $m = 0.03$ and Polaris has $m = 1.98$. How many times more flux do we receive from Vega?
steps: Vega has the smaller magnitude, so it is the brighter one. The difference is $\Delta m = 1.98 - 0.03 = 1.95$.
blocks.a: Vega delivers about $6.0$ times as much flux.

blocks.title: From a flux ratio to magnitudes
blocks.q: A telescope measures that star A delivers 40 times as much flux as star B. What is $m_B - m_A$?
blocks.a: $m_B - m_A \approx 4.0$: B, the fainter star, has the larger magnitude.

blocks.title: Light adds, magnitudes don't
blocks.q: A double star has two members that each have $m = 3.0$. Seen as one point of light, what magnitude does the pair have?
steps: The fluxes add: the pair sends $2F$, where $F$ is one star's flux.
Compare the pair with one star: $m_{\text{pair}} - 3.0 = -2.5\log_{10}(2F/F) = -2.5\log_{10}2 = -0.75$.
blocks.a: $m \approx 2.25$. Adding the magnitudes (to get 6.0) would make the pair look fainter than one star, which can't be right.

blocks.html: Dropping the minus sign. People write $m_1 - m_2 = 2.5\log_{10}(F_1/F_2)$ and find that the brighter star has the larger magnitude. Quick check: after any calculation, the object with more flux must have the smaller magnitude. A second slip is adding magnitudes when light combines; always convert to fluxes, add, and convert back.

Astronomers also use the same logarithm for the Sun ($m = -26.74$) and the faintest galaxies the James Webb Space Telescope can see (around $m = 30$). That range of 57 magnitudes is a flux ratio near $10^{23}$, which is why a logarithmic scale is so handy.

blocks.html: A star's apparent magnitude $m$ depends on two things: how much light it gives out and how far away it is. To compare stars fairly, astronomers define the absolute magnitude $M$: the apparent magnitude the star would have if it sat at a standard distance of 10 parsecs. Combining magnitude arithmetic with the inverse-square law gives a short, powerful formula for distance.

Light spreads over a sphere, so a star of luminosity $L$ at distance $d$ delivers flux $F = L/(4\pi d^2)$. Compare the same star at its real distance $d$ and at 10 pc: $$m - M = -2.5\log_{10}\frac{F(d)}{F(10\text{ pc})} = -2.5\log_{10}\left(\frac{10\text{ pc}}{d}\right)^{2}.$$ The power of 2 comes out of the log as a factor, and $-2.5 \times (-2) = 5$, so $m - M = 5\log_{10}(d/10\text{ pc})$. The luminosity cancels, which is the whole point.
The distance modulus is $$m - M = 5\log_{10}\frac{d}{10\text{ pc}}, \qquad d = 10^{(m - M + 5)/5}\text{ pc}.$$ It depends only on distance (when there is no dust in the way).

blocks.title: The Sun's absolute magnitude
blocks.q: The Sun has $m = -26.74$ at a distance of $1\text{ AU} = 4.848 \times 10^{-6}$ pc. Find its absolute magnitude.
blocks.a: $M_\odot \approx 4.83$. From 10 pc the Sun would be a faint naked-eye star.

blocks.title: A Cepheid in a nearby galaxy
blocks.q: A Cepheid variable with $M = -4.0$ appears at $m = 16.0$. How far away is it?
blocks.a: $d = 1.0 \times 10^{5}$ pc $= 100$ kpc, well outside the disk of the Milky Way.

blocks.title: Predicting how bright a star looks
blocks.q: A star with $M = 1.5$ lies 250 pc away. What is its apparent magnitude?
blocks.a: $m \approx 8.5$, too faint for the naked eye but easy in binoculars.

blocks.html: Putting the distance in light-years. The 10 in the formula is 10 parsecs, so $d$ must be in parsecs too. A star 100 pc away is 326 ly away; plugging in 326 gives $m - M = 7.6$ instead of the correct $5.0$, an error of 2.6 magnitudes. Convert first ($1\text{ pc} = 3.26$ ly). A second slip is writing $5\log_{10}d$ and forgetting the 10 pc, which shifts every answer by 5. Check: a star at exactly 10 pc must come out with $m = M$.

blocks.html: The space between stars is not quite empty. Along with thin gas, it holds tiny solid grains of dust, mostly silicates and carbon compounds, about 0.1 μm across or smaller. Dust dims every star behind it, and it changes the distance modulus: if you forget it, a star looks farther away than it is.

A grain blocks light most effectively when it is about as large as the wavelength or larger. Interstellar grains are comparable to visible wavelengths, so they scatter and absorb short (blue) wavelengths more strongly than long (red) ones; in the visible, the dimming grows roughly as $1/\lambda$. So dust does two things at once. It makes a star fainter (extinction), and because more blue than red light is removed, it makes the light that gets through look redder (reddening). Dust does not erase or move a star's absorption lines, so the spectrum still tells the star's true temperature.

Extinction $A_V$ (in magnitudes) adds to the distance modulus: $$m - M = 5\log_{10}\frac{d}{10\text{ pc}} + A_V.$$ Reddening is the color excess $E(B - V) = (B - V)_{\text{observed}} - (B - V)_0$, and for typical dust in the Milky Way $A_V \approx 3.1\,E(B - V)$.

That last relation is what makes extinction measurable. The spectral lines give the true color $(B - V)_0$ of a star of that type; the photometry gives the observed color; the difference is the reddening, and 3.1 times it is the dimming in the $V$ band.

blocks.title: Correcting a distance for dust
blocks.q: A star has $m_V = 12.0$ and $M_V = 2.0$, and dust dims it by $A_V = 1.5$ mag. How far away is it? How far would you have said if you ignored the dust?
blocks.a: About 500 pc. Ignoring the dust would double the distance.

blocks.title: Measuring the dust from color
blocks.q: A star's spectrum marks it as a type whose true color is $(B - V)_0 = 0.35$, but we measure $B - V = 0.85$. Find $E(B - V)$ and $A_V$.
blocks.a: $E(B - V) = 0.50$ and $A_V \approx 1.6$ mag: the dust cuts the visual flux by a factor of $10^{0.4 \times 1.55} \approx 4$.

blocks.title: Why we look at the galactic center in infrared
blocks.q: Toward the center of the Milky Way, visual extinction is about $A_V \approx 30$ mag. By what factor does dust cut the visible light?
steps: Infrared and radio waves, much longer than the grains, pass through with far less loss.
blocks.a: A factor of about a trillion, so astronomers study the galactic center in infrared, radio and X-rays.

blocks.html: Taking a reddened star to be a cool star. A hot B star seen through thick dust can have the $B - V$ of a cool G or K star. If you read its temperature from color alone, you get it wrong; if you then use a cool star's luminosity, its distance is wrong too. Check the spectral lines: dust reddens the continuum but leaves the pattern of lines, which tells the true temperature, unchanged.

The setting Sun is reddened in the same direction for a related reason: air molecules scatter blue light much more than red. The particles and the wavelength dependence differ, but in both cases the blue is removed from the direct beam.

blocks.html: Your eye sees color, but a telescope measures it with filters. The standard Johnson filters pass bands of light centered near 440 nm (B, blue) and 550 nm (V, visual, yellow-green). Measure a star's magnitude through each, and their difference is its color index $B - V$. It builds directly on magnitude arithmetic.

A difference of two magnitudes is a ratio of two fluxes: $$B - V = -2.5\log_{10}\frac{F_B}{F_V} + \text{const},$$ with the constant chosen so that Vega has $B - V \approx 0$. A hotter blackbody pushes its peak toward the blue, so it sends relatively more light through the B filter than through the V filter. A larger $F_B/F_V$ means a smaller (even negative) $B - V$. Distance dims both bands by the same factor, so it cancels in the ratio: color is a thermometer that works at any distance (as long as no dust is in the way).
$B - V = m_B - m_V$. Smaller $B - V$ means a hotter, bluer star; larger $B - V$ means a cooler, redder one.

blocks.q: Relative to Vega, a star's ratio of blue to visual flux, $F_B/F_V$, is $0.40$ times Vega's. What is its $B - V$?
blocks.a: $B - V \approx 0.99$, an orange K-type star.

blocks.title: Bright is not the same as hot
blocks.q: Star X has $V = 2.0$ and $B - V = 1.5$. Star Y has $V = 8.0$ and $B - V = -0.1$. Which is hotter?
steps: Brightness ($V$) depends on luminosity and distance, not only on temperature, so ignore it here.
Star Y has the smaller color index.
blocks.a: Star Y is hotter (a blue star), even though star X looks 250 times brighter.

blocks.html: Thinking a larger $B - V$ means a bluer star. Remember that magnitudes grow as light gets fainter. A large $B - V$ means $m_B$ is large: the star is faint in blue light compared with yellow-green light, so it is red and cool. Quick check: Betelgeuse, a red supergiant, has $B - V = +1.85$; Spica, a blue-white star, has $-0.23$.
Dust also reddens starlight (see extinction and reddening), so astronomers check colors against spectral lines, which dust does not change.

blocks.html: In Planck and Blackbody Radiation you saw why quantized energies give the blackbody spectrum. Astrophysicists use the result as a working tool. It tells a star's temperature from its color, its power from its size, and it describes the oldest light in the universe.

The Planck function gives the power emitted per unit area, per unit wavelength, per unit solid angle: $$B_\lambda(T) = \frac{2hc^2}{\lambda^5}\,\frac{1}{e^{hc/\lambda kT} - 1}.$$ Its peak gives Wien's law, $\lambda_{\max}T = 2.898 \times 10^{-3}$ m·K, and its area gives the flux $F = \pi\int_0^\infty B_\lambda\,d\lambda = \sigma T^4$.

Write $x = hc/(\lambda kT)$. Then $1/\lambda^5 = (kT/hc)^5x^5$, so at a fixed temperature $$B_\lambda = 2hc^2\left(\frac{kT}{hc}\right)^{5}\frac{x^5}{e^x - 1}.$$ Finding the peak means maximizing $x^5/(e^x - 1)$. Setting the derivative to zero gives $5(e^x - 1) = xe^x$, or $x = 5(1 - e^{-x})$. Start at $x = 5$ and iterate: $5(1 - e^{-5}) = 4.966$, then $4.965$. So the peak sits at $x = 4.965$, which means $\lambda_{\max}T = hc/(4.965\,k) = 2.898 \times 10^{-3}$ m·K. The peak wavelength is inversely proportional to temperature.

Integrate over all wavelengths, substituting $\lambda = hc/(xkT)$: $$\int_0^\infty B_\lambda\,d\lambda = \frac{2k^4T^4}{h^3c^2}\int_0^\infty \frac{x^3}{e^x - 1}\,dx.$$ This is an improper integral, and it converges: near $0$ the integrand behaves like $x^2$, and for large $x$ it dies off like $x^3e^{-x}$. Its value is $\pi^4/15$. Multiplying by $\pi$ (to add up the light leaving a surface in every outward direction) gives $F = \sigma T^4$ with $\sigma = 2\pi^5k^4/(15h^3c^2) = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}$ W/(m²·K⁴). The temperature comes out as $T^4$ because the substitution pulled out $T^5$ from the curve's height and $1/T$ from its width.

blocks.cap: Planck curves at 3,500 K, 5,772 K (the Sun) and 8,000 K. The curves never cross: the hotter body is brighter at every wavelength, and its peak moves toward the blue.

blocks.title: The Sun's peak
blocks.q: Where does the Sun's spectrum ($T = 5772$ K) peak?
blocks.a: About 502 nm, blue-green light. (Plotted per unit frequency instead, the peak lands elsewhere, so "the Sun's peak color" depends on how you plot it.)

blocks.title: Hotter is brighter at every wavelength
blocks.q: At $\lambda = 500$ nm, compare $B_\lambda$ for 8,000 K and 4,000 K. Use $hc/k = 1.4388 \times 10^{-2}$ m·K.
steps: The factor $2hc^2/\lambda^5$ cancels in the ratio; only $1/(e^x - 1)$ changes.
blocks.a: Doubling the temperature raises the 500 nm output about 37 times, far more than 2 times.

blocks.title: The long-wavelength limit
blocks.q: Repeat the comparison at $\lambda = 1$ cm, a radio wavelength.
steps: For small $x$, $e^x - 1 \approx x$, so $B_\lambda \approx 2ckT/\lambda^4$ (the Rayleigh–Jeans law), proportional to $T$.
blocks.a: The ratio is $2.00$: at long wavelengths the hotter body is brighter only in proportion to its temperature.

blocks.html: Thinking a hotter blackbody is brighter only at short wavelengths, because its peak moves to the blue. In fact $B_\lambda$ grows with $T$ at every wavelength: raising $T$ lowers $x = hc/\lambda kT$, which lowers $e^x - 1$ and raises $B_\lambda$. The curves for different temperatures never cross. Check with the examples above: the hotter body wins at 500 nm and at 1 cm.

blocks.html: You already know L = 4πR²σT⁴. Here you will use it with real stars and see just how different they are. A star is not a perfect blackbody, so astronomers define its effective temperature $T_{\text{eff}}$: the temperature a blackbody of the same radius would need to give out the same total power.

Each square meter of a blackbody surface radiates $\sigma T^4$ (the area under the Planck function). A sphere of radius $R$ has $4\pi R^2$ square meters. Multiply: $L = 4\pi R^2\sigma T_{\text{eff}}^4$. That equation defines $T_{\text{eff}}$ once $L$ and $R$ are measured. Dividing by the same equation for the Sun removes $4\pi\sigma$ and leaves a ratio form that is easy to use.

$$\frac{L}{L_\odot} = \left(\frac{R}{R_\odot}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{T_{\text{eff}}}{T_\odot}\right)^{4}, \qquad \frac{R}{R_\odot} = \sqrt{\frac{L}{L_\odot}}\left(\frac{T_\odot}{T_{\text{eff}}}\right)^{2},$$ with $T_\odot = 5772$ K.

blocks.name: ph-hr
blocks.cap: Dashed lines of constant radius run diagonally across the H–R diagram. Giants and supergiants sit above the main sequence because they are huge; white dwarfs sit below because they are tiny.

blocks.title: A red giant
blocks.q: Aldebaran has $L \approx 440\,L_\odot$ and $T_{\text{eff}} \approx 3900$ K. Find its radius.
blocks.a: About $46\,R_\odot$: a cool star can be very luminous only by being very large.

blocks.title: A white dwarf
blocks.q: Sirius B has $T_{\text{eff}} \approx 25{,}000$ K and $R \approx 0.0084\,R_\odot$. Find its luminosity, and its radius in kilometers ($R_\odot = 6.96 \times 10^{5}$ km).
blocks.a: About $0.025\,L_\odot$ from a body smaller than Earth (radius 6,371 km), even though it is four times hotter than the Sun.

blocks.title: A red supergiant
blocks.q: Betelgeuse has $L \approx 1 \times 10^{5}\,L_\odot$ and $T_{\text{eff}} \approx 3600$ K. How big is it?
steps: In kilometers, $810 \times 6.96 \times 10^{5} = 5.6 \times 10^{8}$ km. Divide by $1.496 \times 10^{8}$ km per AU: about $3.8$ AU.
blocks.a: About 800 solar radii, roughly 4 AU. Put in the Sun's place, it would reach past Mars's orbit (1.5 AU) and most of the way to Jupiter's (5.2 AU). (Its luminosity and size are uncertain by tens of percent.)

blocks.html: Forgetting the powers. Temperature enters as the fourth power and radius as the square, so a star twice as hot as the Sun with the same radius is $2^4 = 16$ times as luminous, not 2 times; a star 10 times wider is 100 times as luminous at the same temperature. When solving for $R$, take the square root of $L$ but square the temperature ratio. Check your answer against the H–R diagram: cool and luminous must mean big.

blocks.html: A hydrogen atom can absorb a Balmer photon only if its electron already sits in level $n = 2$ (see Hydrogen's Spectral Series). So the strength of the Balmer lines in a star's spectrum depends on how many hydrogen atoms in its atmosphere are in $n = 2$. Temperature sets that number, and the rule that sets it is one of the most useful in all of physics.

In a gas at temperature $T$, atoms constantly trade energy in collisions. Statistical physics shows that in equilibrium the chance of finding an atom in a particular state of energy $E$ is proportional to the Boltzmann factor $e^{-E/kT}$: each extra $kT$ of energy makes a state $e \approx 2.7$ times less likely. A level can also contain several states with the same energy; its statistical weight $g$ counts them. For hydrogen, level $n$ has $n^2$ orbital states, each with two spin states, so $g_n = 2n^2$.
The Boltzmann equation: $$\frac{N_b}{N_a} = \frac{g_b}{g_a}\,e^{-(E_b - E_a)/kT}.$$ For hydrogen, $N_2/N_1 = 4\,e^{-10.2\text{ eV}/kT}$, with $k = 8.617 \times 10^{-5}$ eV/K.

It does, but above about 10,000 K most hydrogen atoms lose their electron entirely, and an ionized atom cannot absorb a Balmer photon. blocks.html: In the early 1900s Annie Jump Cannon sorted hundreds of thousands of stellar spectra into the classes O, B, A, F, G, K and M, purely by the look of their lines. Were these different kinds of stars, made of different stuff? In 1925 Cecilia Payne showed that their compositions are much alike, dominated by hydrogen and helium; the differences come from temperature. (We now know stars are about three-quarters hydrogen and one-quarter helium by mass.) The key was ionization, which follows on from the Boltzmann equation.

Freeing an electron costs the ionization energy $\chi$ (13.6 eV for hydrogen), so ionization also carries a factor $e^{-\chi/kT}$. But a free electron can be anywhere, with any momentum, so it has a vast number of states open to it, and that number grows as $T^{3/2}$ and as the electron density $n_e$ falls. This huge count of states means atoms ionize at temperatures where $kT$ is only a small fraction of $\chi$, typically a tenth to a twentieth. The result is the Saha equation; for hydrogen it reads $$\frac{N_{\text{II}}}{N_{\text{I}}} = \frac{C\,T^{3/2}}{n_e}\,e^{-\chi/kT}, \qquad C = 2.415 \times 10^{21}\text{ m}^{-3}\text{K}^{-3/2}.$$

Each element and ion has a narrow range of temperature where its lines are strong: hot enough to excite it, not so hot that it is ionized away. So the spectral classes O B A F G K M are a temperature sequence, not a sequence of composition.

blocks.title: How ionized is hydrogen at 10,000 K?
blocks.q: In a stellar atmosphere at $T = 10{,}000$ K with $n_e = 1.0 \times 10^{20}$ m⁻³, find $N_{\text{II}}/N_{\text{I}}$ for hydrogen.

blocks.title: A little cooler

blocks.q: A star shows strong lines of ionized helium. What can you say?
steps: Ionizing helium once takes 24.6 eV, and exciting He II enough to absorb visible light takes even more.
Only the hottest atmospheres have enough energetic collisions and photons.

blocks.html: Thinking stars of different spectral classes are made of different elements. An M star shows titanium oxide bands not because it is rich in titanium, but because it is cool enough for molecules to survive. The Sun shows weak hydrogen lines not because it lacks hydrogen (it is about 74% hydrogen by mass), but because at 5,800 K almost no hydrogen is in level $n = 2$. Check any claim about composition against temperature first.

blocks.html: Almost everything we know about the masses of stars comes from binaries, pairs of stars in orbit around each other. In a visual binary a telescope separates the two stars, and over years or decades you can watch one trace an ellipse around the other. In Binary Stars and Stellar Masses you saw the idea; here you will do the full calculation, using Kepler's third law from Newton.

Newton's version of Kepler's third law for two bodies is $$P^2 = \frac{4\pi^2a^3}{G(M_1 + M_2)},$$ where $a$ is the semi-major axis of the relative orbit (one star around the other). For Earth and the Sun the same law gives $(1\text{ yr})^2 = 4\pi^2(1\text{ AU})^3/(GM_\odot)$. Divide one equation by the other, and $4\pi^2$ and $G$ cancel: with $a$ in AU, $P$ in years and masses in solar masses, $M_1 + M_2 = a^3/P^2$. The catch is that a telescope measures the orbit as an angle $\alpha$ in arcseconds. The parsec is defined so that 1 AU seen from 1 pc spans exactly 1″, so the small-angle rule becomes $a\,(\text{AU}) = \alpha\,('') \times d\,(\text{pc}) = \alpha/p$.

Convert the angle first, then weigh: $$a = \frac{\alpha}{p}\ \text{AU}, \qquad M_1 + M_2 = \frac{a^3}{P^2}\ M_\odot.$$ Each star circles the center of mass, so $M_1a_1 = M_2a_2$: the heavier star moves on the smaller ellipse.

blocks.cap: Two stars around their center of mass. The lighter star swings on the bigger orbit; both share one period. You can launch your own orbits in the Orbit Lab.

blocks.title: Weighing Sirius
blocks.q: Sirius A and its white dwarf companion Sirius B have a relative orbit with angular semi-major axis $7.50''$ and period $50.1$ years. The parallax of Sirius is $0.379''$. Find the total mass.
blocks.a: About $3.1\,M_\odot$ for the pair.

blocks.title: Splitting the mass
blocks.q: Measured against the background stars, Sirius B's orbit around the center of mass is about twice as large as Sirius A's. Find each mass.
blocks.a: Sirius A has about $2.1\,M_\odot$; Sirius B, only Earth-sized, has about $1.0\,M_\odot$.

blocks.title: A pair like our neighbors
blocks.q: The two bright stars of Alpha Centauri orbit each other with $a = 23.4$ AU and $P = 79.9$ yr. What is their total mass?
blocks.a: About $2.0\,M_\odot$, two stars much like the Sun.

blocks.html: Putting the angle straight into Kepler's law. $\alpha = 7.50''$ is not 7.50 AU; Kepler's law needs a length. Using arcseconds as if they were AU here would give $7.5^3/50.1^2 = 0.17\,M_\odot$ instead of $3.1\,M_\odot$. Convert with $a = \alpha/p$ (or $\alpha \times d$ in parsecs) first. Also use the relative orbit, $a = a_1 + a_2$, not one star's orbit around the center of mass.
This is how the mass–luminosity relation was first measured: binaries give masses, and the same stars' distances and brightness give luminosities.

blocks.html: Most binaries are too far away, or too close together, for any telescope to split them. Their spectra still give them away: the lines of each star shift back and forth as it moves toward and away from us. This builds on the Doppler shift of light and on visual binaries.

Both stars circle their center of mass with the same period. If the center of mass is at rest, the total momentum is zero: $M_1v_1 = M_2v_2$. So the star with the larger speed is the lighter one, and the ratio of speeds gives the mass ratio. For circular orbits seen edge-on, each star covers a circle of radius $a_i = v_iP/(2\pi)$, so the separation is $a = (v_1 + v_2)P/(2\pi)$. Kepler's third law, $M_1 + M_2 = 4\pi^2a^3/(GP^2)$, then gives $$M_1 + M_2 = \frac{(v_1 + v_2)^3P}{2\pi G}.$$

Speeds come from Doppler shifts, $v_r = c\,\Delta\lambda/\lambda_0$. The mass ratio is $M_1/M_2 = v_2/v_1$, and for an edge-on orbit $M_1 + M_2 = (v_1 + v_2)^3P/(2\pi G)$. If the tilt $i$ is unknown, the measured speeds are $v\sin i$ and you get $(M_1 + M_2)\sin^3 i$, a lower limit.

blocks.name: ph-orbit
blocks.cap: Radial velocities of the two stars. The curves are mirror images: when one star approaches, the other recedes. The lighter star has the larger swing.

blocks.title: A speed from a shift
blocks.q: The H$\alpha$ line (656.28 nm) of one star in a binary swings back and forth by up to $0.088$ nm. What is the star's speed along our line of sight?
blocks.a: The radial-velocity amplitude is about 40 km/s.

blocks.title: Weighing an eclipsing pair
blocks.q: An eclipsing binary (orbit edge-on, circular) has radial-velocity amplitudes $v_1 = 40$ km/s and $v_2 = 80$ km/s and period $P = 10.0$ days. Find the separation and both masses.
steps: Mass ratio: $M_1/M_2 = v_2/v_1 = 2.0$; star 1 is the heavier one.
blocks.a: $a = 0.110$ AU; $M_1 \approx 1.2\,M_\odot$, $M_2 \approx 0.60\,M_\odot$.

blocks.title: When the tilt is unknown
blocks.q: Suppose the same speeds were measured for a binary with no eclipses, and later the tilt turned out to be $i = 60^\circ$. What are the true total mass and the masses?
steps: The measured speeds were $v\sin i$, so the formula gave $(M_1 + M_2)\sin^3 i = 1.79\,M_\odot$.
blocks.a: About $2.8\,M_\odot$ in all: $1.8$ and $0.92\,M_\odot$. The ratio is unchanged.

blocks.html: Thinking the faster-moving star is the heavier one. It is the other way around: the heavier star sits closer to the center of mass and moves on a smaller, slower circle. Check with $M_1v_1 = M_2v_2$: a large speed must go with a small mass. (A planet and its star are the extreme case: the star barely moves.)

blocks.html: If we happen to see a binary's orbit almost edge-on, the stars take turns passing in front of each other, and the total light dips twice each orbit. Algol in Perseus does this: every 2.87 days it fades by more than a magnitude over several hours, when its larger, cooler companion covers the hot main star. Combined with the speeds from spectroscopic binaries, eclipses measure the sizes of stars directly.

Picture a small star of radius $R_s$ crossing behind a large star of radius $R_\ell$ at relative speed $v$. Label four moments: first contact $t_a$; the small star just fully hidden $t_b$; it starts to reappear $t_c$; last contact $t_d$. Between $t_a$ and $t_b$ the small star slides its own diameter, so $2R_s = v(t_b - t_a)$. Between $t_a$ and $t_c$ its leading edge crosses the whole large star, so $2R_\ell = v(t_c - t_a)$. For the depths, use the fact that each square meter of a star's surface shines in proportion to $T^4$. In both eclipses (when one disk lies completely across the other) the hidden area is the same, $\pi R_s^2$. Only the surface that gets hidden differs.

$R_s = \tfrac12 v(t_b - t_a)$ and $R_\ell = \tfrac12 v(t_c - t_a)$. The deeper, primary eclipse hides the hotter star's surface, and $$\frac{\text{primary depth}}{\text{secondary depth}} = \left(\frac{T_{\text{hot}}}{T_{\text{cool}}}\right)^{4}.$$

blocks.name: astrophys-eclipse

opts.task: Play the orbit, or drag the phase, and watch which eclipse is deeper. Then make the small star cooler.

blocks.cap: A large cool giant and a small hot star. Phase 0: the hot star crosses the giant; phase 0.5: it hides behind the giant. The same area is covered both times, but hiding the hotter surface removes more light.

blocks.title: Sizes from timing
blocks.q: In an edge-on binary the relative speed is 300 km/s. The small star takes 1.5 h from first contact to full eclipse, and 9.0 h from first contact until it begins to reappear. Find both radii.
blocks.a: About $1.2\,R_\odot$ and $7.0\,R_\odot$.

blocks.title: Temperatures from depths
blocks.q: A binary's primary eclipse removes 50% of the light and its secondary removes 8%. Both are total or annular. What is $T_{\text{hot}}/T_{\text{cool}}$?
blocks.a: The hotter star is about 1.6 times hotter.

blocks.title: Which eclipse is deeper?
blocks.q: A small B star (20,000 K) orbits a large K giant (4,500 K). Which eclipse is the primary one?
steps: Either way the hidden area is the B star's disk.

When the B star goes behind the giant, we lose a disk of 20,000 K surface. When it passes in front, we lose a disk of 4,500 K surface: $(20{,}000/4500)^4 \approx 390$ times less light per square meter.
blocks.a: The primary (deep) eclipse is when the small hot star is hidden behind the giant.

blocks.html: Thinking the deeper eclipse happens when the bigger star is hidden. The bigger star is never fully hidden; in both eclipses the same area, the small star's disk, is covered. The depth depends on the surface brightness ($\propto T^4$) of whichever surface is covered, so the primary eclipse always hides the hotter star. Check: if both stars had the same temperature, the two eclipses would be equally deep.
Real stars are darker near their edges (limb darkening), which rounds the bottoms of the dips. Fitting that shape refines the radii.

blocks.html: A planet that crosses in front of its star is a tiny eclipsing binary in which one member is dark. You met the idea in Finding Planets Around Other Stars, and the geometry of eclipsing binaries carries over. NASA's Kepler and TESS missions found thousands of planets this way by watching stars dim on a schedule.

The star's disk has area $\pi R_\star^2$ and the planet covers $\pi R_p^2$ of it. If the disk were uniformly bright, the fraction of light lost would be the ratio of areas: $$\delta = \frac{\pi R_p^2}{\pi R_\star^2} = \left(\frac{R_p}{R_\star}\right)^{2}.$$ The repeat time is the orbital period, and Kepler's third law turns it into the orbit's size: $a^3 = M_\star P^2$ (AU, years, solar masses). During a central transit the planet moves a distance $2R_\star$ at its orbital speed $2\pi a/P$, which gives the transit's length.
Depth $\delta = (R_p/R_\star)^2$, so $R_p = R_\star\sqrt{\delta}$. Period gives $a = (M_\star P^2)^{1/3}$, and a central transit lasts about $t \approx PR_\star/(\pi a)$.

blocks.cap: A dark planet with one-tenth of the star's radius blocks one-hundredth of its light: $(0.1)^2 = 1\%$.

blocks.cap: Depths an observer far away would see. Earth-size planets around Sun-like stars dim them by less than one part in 10,000.

blocks.title: An Earth-size planet
blocks.q: A star of $0.90\,R_\odot$ dims by 100 parts per million during each transit. How big is the planet? ($R_\odot = 109\,R_\oplus$.)
blocks.a: About the size of Earth.

blocks.title: Orbit and duration
blocks.q: A planet transits a $1.0\,M_\odot$, $1.0\,R_\odot$ star every 3.5 days. Find its orbital radius and how long a central transit lasts ($1\text{ AU} = 215\,R_\odot$).
blocks.a: $a \approx 0.045$ AU (a "hot Jupiter" distance, far inside Mercury's 0.39 AU), and each transit lasts about 2.8 hours.

blocks.title: What is it made of?
blocks.q: Another transiting planet has a radius of $1.5\,R_\oplus$, and the wobble it gives its star yields a mass of $5.0\,M_\oplus$. Find its mean density. (Earth's mean density is 5.51 g/cm³.)
steps: Density scales as mass over radius cubed: $\rho = 5.51 \times 5.0/1.5^3$ g/cm³.
blocks.a: About 8.2 g/cm³, denser than Earth: a rocky planet, probably with a large iron core. Combining transits (size) with wobbles (mass) is how astronomers tell rocky worlds from gas-rich ones.

blocks.html: Taking the depth to be $R_p/R_\star$ instead of its square. A dip of 1% does not mean the planet is 1% of the star's radius; it means $R_p/R_\star = \sqrt{0.01} = 0.1$, ten times larger. The light lost depends on the area covered. Check: Jupiter, about one-tenth of the Sun's radius, would cause a 1% dip, not a 10% one.

blocks.html: A planet does not simply orbit its star. Both orbit their common center of mass, so the star makes a small, slow orbit of its own. That motion shows up as a tiny Doppler shift in the star's spectrum, the same method as for spectroscopic binaries with one invisible partner. In 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found 51 Pegasi b this way, the first planet around a Sun-like star.

Momentum about the center of mass balances: $M_\star v_\star = m_pv_p$. For a light planet on a circular orbit, Kepler's third law gives the planet's speed: $a^3 = GM_\star P^2/(4\pi^2)$ and $v_p = 2\pi a/P = (2\pi GM_\star/P)^{1/3}$. We see only the part of the star's velocity along our line of sight, $K = v_\star\sin i$, where $i$ is the tilt of the orbit ($90^\circ$ is edge-on). Putting these together, $$K = \frac{m_p\sin i}{M_\star}\left(\frac{2\pi GM_\star}{P}\right)^{1/3}, \qquad m_p\sin i = K\,M_\star^{2/3}\left(\frac{P}{2\pi G}\right)^{1/3}.$$
The radial-velocity method measures $m_p\sin i$, the planet's minimum mass. The true mass is $m_p = (m_p\sin i)/\sin i$, which is larger unless the orbit is edge-on.

blocks.name: ph-orbit
blocks.cap: A heavy star and a light companion. The star's small circle and small velocity swing are what the radial-velocity method detects.

blocks.title: The Sun's wobble from Jupiter
blocks.q: Jupiter ($1.90 \times 10^{27}$ kg) orbits the Sun ($1.99 \times 10^{30}$ kg) at 13.1 km/s. How fast does the Sun move around their center of mass?
steps: The mass ratio is $1.90 \times 10^{27}/1.99 \times 10^{30} = 9.55 \times 10^{-4}$, so $v_\odot = 9.55 \times 10^{-4} \times 13{,}100$ m/s.
blocks.a: About 12.5 m/s, about as fast as the fastest human sprinters, repeating every 11.9 years. Earth moves the Sun by only 9 cm/s.

blocks.title: 51 Pegasi b
blocks.q: 51 Pegasi ($1.11\,M_\odot$) wobbles with $K = 56$ m/s and period 4.23 days. Find $m\sin i$ in Jupiter masses.
blocks.a: About $0.48\,M_\text{J}$, a Jupiter-like planet orbiting closer to its star than Mercury does to the Sun.

blocks.title: Adding the tilt
blocks.q: A planet has $m\sin i = 2.0\,M_\text{J}$. Measurements of the star's position on the sky show the orbit is tilted $i = 30^\circ$ from face-on. What is its true mass?
blocks.a: $4.0\,M_\text{J}$, twice the minimum.

blocks.html: Treating $m\sin i$ as the planet's mass. Doppler shifts see only motion toward or away from us. A planet on a nearly face-on orbit barely shifts its star's lines, so it can look light when it is heavy. The radial-velocity mass is a lower limit. A planet that also transits has $i \approx 90^\circ$, so for it $m\sin i$ is close to the true mass. Check: $\sin i \le 1$, so the true mass can never be less than $m\sin i$.

blocks.html: How warm is a planet? To first order, it settles at the temperature where the starlight it absorbs balances the heat it radiates away. This uses the Stefan–Boltzmann law twice, once for the star and once for the planet, and the planet sizes from transits drop out.

At distance $d$ the star's flux is $L/(4\pi d^2)$. The planet intercepts it over its cross-section $\pi R_p^2$ and reflects a fraction $A$ (the albedo), so it absorbs $(1 - A)\dfrac{L}{4\pi d^2}\pi R_p^2$. If it spins fast enough to keep one temperature all over, it radiates from its whole surface, $4\pi R_p^2\sigma T^4$. Set them equal; $R_p$ cancels: $$T^4 = \frac{(1 - A)L}{16\pi\sigma d^2}.$$ Writing $L = 4\pi R_\star^2\sigma T_\star^4$ gives $$T = T_\star(1 - A)^{1/4}\sqrt{\frac{R_\star}{2d}}.$$ For the Sun, the first form becomes $T = 278\text{ K} \times [(1 - A)L/L_\odot]^{1/4}(d/1\text{ AU})^{-1/2}$.

A planet's equilibrium temperature depends on the star (its $T_\star$ and $R_\star$, or its $L$), the distance (as $d^{-1/2}$) and the albedo (as $(1 - A)^{1/4}$), not on the planet's size. An atmosphere can then raise the surface temperature above it (the greenhouse effect).

blocks.name: ph-blackbody
blocks.cap: The Sun (5,772 K) and Earth's equilibrium temperature (255 K) on log axes. Sunlight comes in at visible wavelengths; Earth sends its heat back out in the infrared, near 11 μm.

blocks.title: Earth
blocks.q: Find Earth's equilibrium temperature: $T_\odot = 5772$ K, $R_\odot = 6.96 \times 10^{8}$ m, $d = 1.496 \times 10^{11}$ m, $A = 0.30$.
blocks.a: About 255 K ($-18$ °C). Earth's average surface is about 288 K; the difference of roughly 33 K is the greenhouse effect of its atmosphere.

blocks.title: Mars
blocks.q: Mars orbits at 1.52 AU with albedo about 0.25. Estimate its equilibrium temperature.
blocks.a: About 210 K, close to the average temperature measured on Mars, whose thin atmosphere adds little warming.

blocks.title: Earth's twin around a dim star
blocks.q: A red dwarf has $L = 0.040\,L_\odot$. At what distance would a planet receive the same flux Earth gets from the Sun?
steps: Equal flux means $L/d^2 = L_\odot/(1\text{ AU})^2$, so $d = \sqrt{L/L_\odot}$ AU.
blocks.a: 0.20 AU, closer than Mercury is to the Sun. Habitable zones of dim stars are small and close in, scaling as $\sqrt{L}$.

blocks.html: Thinking distance alone sets a planet's temperature. The star's luminosity matters (as $L^{1/4}$), and so does the albedo: a bright, cloudy planet reflects most of the light it gets. Venus, cloaked in white clouds with $A \approx 0.76$, has an equilibrium temperature of only about 230 K, lower than Earth's, yet its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere holds its surface near 737 K, hotter than Mercury's. Check every claim with all three inputs: the star, the distance and the albedo, and then ask about the atmosphere.

The habitable zone is the range of distances where a planet with a suitable atmosphere could keep liquid water on its surface. Its edges depend on models of atmospheres, so estimates differ, but for the Sun they run from a little inside Earth's orbit to roughly Mars's.

blocks.html: A star is a ball of hot gas that neither collapses under its own weight nor flies apart. Every layer is in balance: the pressure underneath pushes up exactly as hard as gravity and the pressure above push down. You know this idea from pressure and depth in a lake, $\Delta P = \rho g\,\Delta h$. In a star, $g$ changes with depth, and the shell theorem tells us how.

Take a thin slab of gas at radius $r$, with area $A$ and thickness $dr$. Its mass is $\rho A\,dr$. By the shell theorem, only the mass $m(r)$ inside radius $r$ pulls on it, as if all of that mass sat at the center: the weight is $Gm(r)\rho A\,dr/r^2$, pointing inward. The pressure below, $P(r)$, pushes out on the slab's lower face; the pressure above, $P(r + dr)$, pushes in on its upper face. Balance: $$\big[P(r) - P(r + dr)\big]A = \frac{Gm(r)\rho A\,dr}{r^2}.$$ Divide by $A\,dr$ and let $dr \to 0$.

Hydrostatic equilibrium: $$\frac{dP}{dr} = -\frac{Gm(r)\,\rho(r)}{r^2}.$$ Pressure must fall with radius, steeply where gravity and density are large. Hot gas pressure, not a solid core, holds a star up.

blocks.name: ph-star
blocks.cap: A thin layer of gas inside a star. The pressure from below is larger than the pressure from above by just enough to hold up the layer's weight.

blocks.html: For a model star of uniform density, $m(r) = Mr^3/R^3$ and $\rho = 3M/(4\pi R^3)$, so $dP/dr = -\dfrac{3GM^2}{4\pi R^6}\,r$. Integrating from the surface, where $P = 0$, inward gives $P(r) = P_c\,(1 - r^2/R^2)$ with $$P_c = \frac{3GM^2}{8\pi R^4}.$$ Real stars are much denser at the center, so their central pressures are higher.

blocks.title: The pressure gradient inside the Sun
blocks.q: Halfway out in the Sun, $m(r) \approx 0.97\,M_\odot$ and $\rho \approx 1300$ kg/m³. How fast does pressure fall with radius there?
steps: $g \approx 1060$ m/s², about 110 times Earth's surface gravity.
blocks.a: About $1.4 \times 10^{6}$ Pa per meter, roughly 14 atmospheres for each meter you go down.

blocks.title: A uniform Sun
blocks.q: Estimate the Sun's central pressure as if its density were uniform.
blocks.a: About $10^{14}$ Pa, a billion atmospheres. Solar models, with a dense core, give about $2.5 \times 10^{16}$ Pa.

blocks.title: Scaling
blocks.q: Star B has twice the mass and twice the radius of star A, with the same structure. Compare their central pressures.
blocks.a: $P_{c,B} = \tfrac14 P_{c,A}$: the bigger star is less squeezed in its middle.

blocks.html: Picturing a star held up by a solid core, like a planet. The Sun is gas (plasma) all the way to the center, where the density is about 150 times water's and still a gas, because it is so hot. What holds every layer up is the pressure difference across it, which comes from hot, dense gas. Check the logic: if there were no pressure gradient, nothing would stop the layers from falling inward in a free-fall time of under an hour.

blocks.html: Hydrostatic equilibrium plus the ideal gas law is enough to estimate what the center of a star is like, without solving a single differential equation. Astrophysicists call this an order-of-magnitude estimate: replace every derivative by a ratio of typical sizes and keep only the physics.

In $dP/dr = -Gm\rho/r^2$, replace $dP/dr$ by $P_c/R$, $m$ by $M$, $r$ by $R$, and $\rho$ by $M/R^3$. Then $P_c/R \sim GM(M/R^3)/R^2$, so $P_c \sim GM^2/R^4$. The gas is ideal, so $P = nkT$ with particle density $n = \rho/(\mu m_p)$, where $\mu$ is the mean mass of a particle in units of $m_p$ (about 0.6 for ionized solar gas). Then $$kT_c = \frac{P_c\,\mu m_p}{\rho} \sim \frac{GM^2/R^4}{M/R^3}\,\mu m_p = \frac{GM\mu m_p}{R}.$$ It says something simple: a particle at the center has thermal energy comparable to the gravitational energy per particle, $GMm_p/R$. That is what it takes to hold the star up, which is why the core must be hot (see temperature and molecular energy).

$$P_c \sim \frac{GM^2}{R^4}, \qquad T_c \sim \frac{GM\mu m_p}{kR}.$$ For the Sun these give about $10^{15}$ Pa and $10^{7}$ K, close to detailed models (about $2.5 \times 10^{16}$ Pa and $1.57 \times 10^{7}$ K).

blocks.name: ph-star
blocks.cap: Temperature and density inside the Sun from a standard solar model. The center is over 15 million K, against 5,772 K at the surface.

blocks.title: The Sun's core temperature
blocks.q: Estimate $T_c$ for the Sun from $kT_c \sim GMm_p/R$.
blocks.a: Tens of millions of kelvins; models give 15.7 million K.

blocks.title: Temperature from pressure and density
blocks.q: Solar models give the Sun's center $P = 2.5 \times 10^{16}$ Pa and $\rho = 1.5 \times 10^{5}$ kg/m³, with $\mu \approx 0.85$ (the core is now rich in helium). What temperature does the ideal gas law give?
blocks.a: About $1.7 \times 10^{7}$ K, consistent with the models' 15.7 million K.

blocks.title: Bigger stars are only a little hotter inside
blocks.q: On the main sequence $R \propto M^{0.8}$ roughly. How does $T_c$ scale with mass?
blocks.a: Only about 1.6 times the Sun's central temperature, yet, as later topics show, thousands of times its luminosity.

blocks.html: Thinking the Sun's center is about as hot as its surface, as if the Sun were the same all through. Gravity squeezes the inner layers under the weight of everything above, and gas under that pressure must be hot to push back: about 15.7 million K at the center against 5,772 K at the surface. Check with the estimate: $GMm_p/(kR)$ is millions of kelvins, so a cool interior could not hold the Sun up.

blocks.html: Here is one of the strangest facts about stars: when a star loses energy, it gets hotter. The reason is a balance law called the virial theorem, which you have already met in disguise. In orbital energy, a circular orbit has $E = -K$, so a satellite that loses energy to air drag drops lower and speeds up. A star is a swarm of particles held by their own gravity, and the same rule applies.

Multiply hydrostatic equilibrium, $dP = -Gm\rho\,dr/r^2$, by $4\pi r^3$ (three times the volume inside $r$) and add it up over the whole star. On the right, with $dm = 4\pi r^2\rho\,dr$, you get $-\int Gm\,dm/r = U$, the star's gravitational energy. On the left, integrating by parts (with $P = 0$ at the surface) gives $-3\int P\,dV$. For an ideal monatomic gas, pressure is two-thirds of the kinetic energy per unit volume, so $3\int P\,dV = 2K$, where $K$ is the total thermal kinetic energy. Therefore $$2K + U = 0.$$

For a gas ball in equilibrium held by its own gravity: $2K + U = 0$, so $K = -U/2$ and the total energy is $E = K + U = U/2 = -K$. Radiating energy ($E$ falls) makes $K$ rise: the star contracts and heats up. Half of the gravitational energy released is radiated; the other half heats the gas.

blocks.name: ph-star
blocks.cap: A contracting cloud. As gravity releases energy, half goes into heating the gas and half is radiated away, so the cloud gets hotter while it shines.

blocks.title: Energy bookkeeping
blocks.q: A protostar radiates $1.0 \times 10^{38}$ J while staying in equilibrium. How do $K$ and $U$ change?
steps: $\Delta K = -\Delta E = +1.0 \times 10^{38}$ J; $\Delta U = 2\Delta E = -2.0 \times 10^{38}$ J.
blocks.a: Gravity releases $2.0 \times 10^{38}$ J: half heats the star, half leaves as light.

blocks.title: The Sun's thermal energy
blocks.q: For a uniform sphere, $U = -\tfrac35GM^2/R$. Find $U$ and $K$ for a uniform Sun.
blocks.a: $K = -U/2 \approx 1.1 \times 10^{41}$ J of thermal energy. (The real Sun is more centrally concentrated, so both are a few times larger.)

blocks.title: An average temperature
blocks.q: With $K = \tfrac32NkT$ and $N = M/(\mu m_p)$, find the mean temperature of a uniform Sun with $\mu = 0.6$.
blocks.a: About $2.8 \times 10^{6}$ K: millions of kelvins on average.

blocks.html: Thinking a star that radiates energy must cool down, like a cooling cup of coffee. Coffee is not held together by its own gravity. A star is: losing energy lets it contract, contraction releases gravitational energy, and the virial theorem sends half of that into heat. So stars and protostars heat up as they lose energy, a "negative heat capacity". Check against orbits: a satellite slowed by drag ends up moving faster, for exactly the same reason.
This is how a protostar's core gets hot enough to start fusion, and how a star's core heats up to burn helium after its hydrogen runs out.

blocks.html: Before anyone knew about nuclear energy, physicists asked what keeps the Sun shining. Chemical burning would last only thousands of years. In the 1850s and 1860s Hermann von Helmholtz and Lord Kelvin proposed the best idea then available: slow contraction, releasing gravitational energy, as the virial theorem describes.

A star of mass $M$ and radius $R$ has gravitational energy of order $GM^2/R$. By the virial theorem, about half of what contraction releases can be radiated. Divide the available energy by the rate at which it is spent, the luminosity $L$, and you get a time: $$t_{KH} \sim \frac{GM^2}{RL}.$$ For a uniform sphere the radiated energy available from collapsing from far away is $\tfrac{3}{10}GM^2/R$, which shortens the time by about a factor of 3; the order of magnitude is what matters.

The Kelvin–Helmholtz time $t_{KH} \approx GM^2/(RL)$ is about 30 million years for the Sun, far shorter than Earth's age of about 4.5 billion years. Gravity cannot be the Sun's main power source, though it does power protostars before fusion begins.

blocks.name: ph-star
blocks.cap: Contraction as a power source: the cloud heats and shines as it shrinks, but the supply runs out in tens of millions of years.

blocks.title: The Sun
blocks.q: Find $GM^2/(RL)$ for the Sun.
blocks.a: About 31 million years.

blocks.title: Fusion's supply
blocks.q: The Sun will fuse about 10% of its mass, and fusion turns 0.7% of that mass into energy. How long can that last at today's luminosity?
blocks.a: About 10 billion years, roughly 300 times the Kelvin–Helmholtz time.

blocks.title: How fast would the Sun have to shrink?
blocks.q: If contraction alone powered the Sun (uniform sphere, radiated energy $\tfrac{3}{10}GM^2/R$), how fast would its radius shrink?
blocks.a: About 74 m per year: too slow to notice in a human lifetime, but fatal over geological time.

blocks.html: Thinking the Sun could shine for billions of years just by shrinking. The gravitational energy is large but not large enough: at the Sun's luminosity it lasts only a few tens of millions of years. That clashed with geology and with Darwin's estimates of the time evolution needed, and radioactive dating later gave Earth an age of about 4.5 billion years. Check: compare $GM^2/(RL)$ with the age of Earth; they differ by a factor of over 100.

blocks.html: The Sun turns hydrogen into helium, as you saw in How the Sun Shines. The energy comes from the difference in mass, worked out as in energy in nuclear reactions. But four protons never fuse in a single collision; the change happens through a chain of two-particle reactions.

Using atomic masses (which include electrons, so the energy of the positrons annihilating is counted for you): $4 \times 1.007825\text{ u} = 4.031300$ u before, $4.002603$ u after. The missing $0.028697$ u is $0.71\%$ of the mass, and at 931.5 MeV per u it is $26.7$ MeV. A small part of that, on average about $0.6$ MeV in the Sun's main branch, leaves with neutrinos.

items: $p + p \to {}^{2}\text{H} + e^+ + \nu_e$ (needs the weak force to turn a proton into a neutron, so it is very slow)
$^{3}\text{He} + {}^{3}\text{He} \to {}^{4}\text{He} + 2p$ (each of the first two steps happens twice)

blocks.html: Net: $4p \to {}^{4}\text{He} + 2e^+ + 2\nu_e$, releasing $26.7$ MeV. In the CNO cycle, carbon-12 captures four protons in turn (with two beta-plus decays) and ends as carbon-12 plus a helium-4 nucleus: carbon, nitrogen and oxygen are catalysts. The CNO cycle is very sensitive to temperature and dominates in stars above about 1.3 solar masses; in the Sun it supplies about 1% of the energy.

blocks.title: The Sun's fuel budget
blocks.q: How many helium nuclei does the Sun make each second, and how much hydrogen does it use? ($L = 3.83 \times 10^{26}$ W, $1\text{ MeV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-13}$ J.)
blocks.a: About $9 \times 10^{37}$ helium nuclei and 600 million tonnes of hydrogen per second; $L/c^2 = 4.3 \times 10^{9}$ kg of mass becomes energy each second.

blocks.title: One step of the CNO cycle
blocks.q: Find $Q$ for $^{12}\text{C} + {}^{1}\text{H} \to {}^{13}\text{N} + \gamma$, with $m(^{13}\text{N}) = 13.005739$ u.
blocks.a: About $1.94$ MeV, carried off by the gamma ray.

blocks.html: Thinking stars fuse four protons at once in a single collision. Four particles meeting at one point at one instant essentially never happens. Fusion goes through two-particle steps, and the first step of the pp chain is so slow (a proton in the Sun's core waits billions of years on average to make one) that the Sun burns its fuel gradually instead of exploding. Check any proposed reaction: count only two nuclei on the left.

blocks.html: Two protons repel each other electrically. To fuse, they must come within about a femtometer ($10^{-15}$ m), where the strong nuclear force grabs them. You saw in estimating a star's center that the Sun's core is at about 15.7 million K. Is that hot enough? Classically, not even close. The rescue is quantum tunneling.

The Coulomb barrier at separation $r$ is $U = kZ_1Z_2e^2/r$, with $ke^2 = 1.44$ MeV·fm. For two protons at about 1 fm, $U \approx 1.4$ MeV. In the core, $kT = (8.617 \times 10^{-5}\text{ eV/K})(1.57 \times 10^{7}\text{ K}) = 1.35$ keV, about a thousand times less. Even counting the fast tail of the Maxwell distribution, the fraction of protons with 1 MeV goes as $e^{-E/kT} = e^{-740}$: zero for all practical purposes. Quantum mechanics changes the question. A proton's wave function leaks into the barrier, and the probability of getting through falls off as $$P \approx e^{-\sqrt{E_G/E}}, \qquad E_G = 2m_rc^2(\pi\alpha Z_1Z_2)^2,$$ where $m_r$ is the reduced mass and $\alpha \approx 1/137$. For two protons $E_G \approx 493$ keV.

The Sun's core is about a thousand times too cool for protons to climb over the Coulomb barrier. Protons fuse only by tunneling through it, and mostly at energies of a few times $kT$ (the Gamow peak, about 6 keV in the Sun), where enough protons are fast and the tunneling chance is no longer hopeless.

blocks.name: ph-quantum
blocks.cap: The potential energy of two protons against their separation: electric repulsion outside about 1.5 fm, nuclear attraction inside. The dashed line is the typical thermal energy in the Sun's core.

blocks.title: How far short is the core?
blocks.q: Compare the barrier for two protons at 1.0 fm with $kT$ at 15.7 million K.
blocks.a: $U/kT \approx 1060$. Classically, protons would need about $1.7 \times 10^{10}$ K to reach the barrier with typical energies.

blocks.title: The tunneling factor
blocks.q: Using $E_G = 493$ keV for two protons, find the tunneling factor at $E = kT = 1.35$ keV and at $E = 6$ keV.
blocks.a: Tiny, but not zero, and much larger for the faster protons. With about $10^{56}$ protons in the core, tiny is enough.

blocks.title: A quantum estimate of the temperature needed
blocks.q: Suppose fusion becomes possible when a proton's de Broglie wavelength $h/p$ reaches the closest-approach distance $ke^2/E$. With $E = p^2/(2m_r) = \tfrac32kT$ and $m_r = m_p/2$, what temperature is needed?
blocks.a: About $1 \times 10^{7}$ K, right where the Sun's core is. Quantum mechanics lowers the requirement by a factor of about a thousand.

blocks.html: Thinking the Sun's core is hot enough for protons to climb over the Coulomb barrier. Typical protons there have about 1 keV, against a barrier near 1 MeV. When Arthur Eddington proposed in 1920 that stars run on hydrogen fusion, critics objected that stars are not hot enough; tunneling, worked out by George Gamow in 1928 and applied to stars soon after, answered them. Check: compare $kT$ in keV with the barrier in MeV before calling anything "hot enough".

blocks.html: Energy made in the core has to get out. In the Sun's inner region it travels as light, but not in a straight line: the gas is so dense that a photon is absorbed or scattered after a tiny distance, the mean free path $\ell$, and sent off again in a random direction. Building on the conditions at the center, we can estimate how long the trip takes.

Each step is a vector $\vec{s}_i$ of length $\ell$ in a random direction. After $N$ steps the displacement is $\vec{D} = \sum \vec{s}_i$, so $$D^2 = \sum_i s_i^2 + \sum_{i \ne j}\vec{s}_i \cdot \vec{s}_j.$$ The cross terms are as often negative as positive and average to zero, leaving $D^2 \approx N\ell^2$, or $D \approx \sqrt{N}\,\ell$. To cover a distance $R$ takes $N = (R/\ell)^2$ steps, a total path of $N\ell = R^2/\ell$, and a time $t \approx R^2/(\ell c)$.

A random walk of $N$ steps covers only about $\sqrt{N}\,\ell$. Crossing a star of radius $R$ takes $t \approx R^2/(\ell c)$, which is $R/\ell$ times longer than a straight flight. For the Sun the answer is on the order of $10^{5}$ years.

blocks.name: ph-star
blocks.cap: A photon's random walk. After $N$ steps it is typically only $\sqrt{N}$ step lengths from where it began.

blocks.html: In the Sun, energy diffuses outward by radiation from the core to about 0.7 of the radius. Farther out the gas is cooler and far more opaque, and radiation would need a very steep temperature drop to carry the energy. Instead the gas churns: hot blobs rise, cool and sink, in the convective zone, whose tops you can see as granules on the surface. Stars more massive than about 1.3 Suns have convective cores (their energy is made in a small, very hot region); stars below about 0.35 solar masses are convective all the way through.

blocks.title: Counting steps
blocks.q: How many random steps of 1 cm does it take to get 1 m from the start?

blocks.title: Escaping the Sun
blocks.q: With an average mean free path of 1 mm, how long does energy take to random-walk out of the Sun? ($R = 6.96 \times 10^{8}$ m.)
blocks.a: About 51,000 years. With $\ell = 0.5$ mm, about 100,000 years. A straight flight would take 2.3 seconds.

blocks.title: Where the mean free path comes from
blocks.q: Photons scatter off free electrons with cross-section $\sigma_T = 6.65 \times 10^{-29}$ m². What is $\ell$ where $n_e = 1.0 \times 10^{30}$ m⁻³?
blocks.a: $\ell \approx 1.5$ cm. Deeper in, densities are higher and absorption by ions adds to the scattering, so the average step in the Sun is much shorter.

blocks.html: Thinking light made in the core reaches the surface in a few seconds because it travels at the speed of light. Each photon goes only about a millimeter or so before it is absorbed and re-emitted in a random direction, so the energy wanders outward slowly; estimates for the Sun range from tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand years, depending on the model. Check with $D = \sqrt{N}\,\ell$: doubling the distance takes four times as many steps.

blocks.html: Binary stars (see masses from visual binaries) let astronomers measure masses, and for main-sequence stars a striking pattern appears: luminosity rises very steeply with mass. That explains the main-sequence lifetimes you met before, and it follows from energy transport.

Energy diffuses out by radiation. The luminosity is roughly the radiant energy stored, which grows as $T^4$, times the volume, divided by the time it takes to random-walk out, $R^2/(\ell c)$. With the mean free path $\ell = 1/(\kappa\rho)$ (opacity $\kappa$), $\rho \sim M/R^3$ and $T \sim GM\mu m_p/(kR)$ from the central-conditions estimate: $$L \sim \frac{aT^4R^3 \cdot \ell c}{R^2} \sim \frac{ac}{\kappa}\,\frac{T^4R^4}{M} \propto \frac{(M/R)^4R^4}{M} = M^3.$$ The radius cancels. Opacity that changes with temperature and density steepens this a little, so on the main sequence roughly $L \propto M^{3.5}$.

For main-sequence stars, roughly $L/L_\odot \approx (M/M_\odot)^{3.5}$. A star's fuel is proportional to $M$, so its lifetime goes as $M/L \propto M^{-2.5}$: about $10\text{ Gyr} \times (M/M_\odot)^{-2.5}$.

blocks.name: ph-hr
blocks.cap: Luminosity against mass for main-sequence stars on log axes. The slope is about 3.5 for Sun-like and moderately massive stars; it is less steep for the smallest and the most massive stars.

blocks.title: A two-solar-mass star
blocks.q: Find the luminosity and main-sequence lifetime of a $2\,M_\odot$ star.
blocks.a: About $11\,L_\odot$ and 1.8 Gyr: twice the fuel, burned eleven times as fast.

blocks.title: A massive star
blocks.q: Repeat for $10\,M_\odot$.
blocks.a: About 3,200 $L_\odot$ and 32 million years. (Very massive stars fall below the $M^{3.5}$ line, but the trend holds.)

blocks.title: Dating a cluster
blocks.q: A cluster's main-sequence turnoff is at $2.0\,M_\odot$. About how old is it?
steps: The turnoff stars are just ending their lives: $t = 10 \times 2.0^{-2.5}$ Gyr.
blocks.a: About 1.8 billion years.

blocks.html: The relation is a rough guide. Below about half a solar mass it is shallower (stars there are partly or fully convective), and above about 50 solar masses luminosity rises only about in proportion to mass, because those stars approach the limit in the next topic. The smallest stars, near 0.08 solar masses, shine at about a thousandth of the Sun's luminosity or less and will last for trillions of years.

Thinking a star twice as massive is twice as luminous. Mass sets the central temperature and how easily energy escapes, and luminosity responds steeply: twice the mass gives about $2^{3.5} \approx 11$ times the luminosity. So massive stars, despite having more fuel, die far sooner. Check: the most massive stars live only a few million years, while the smallest red dwarfs will outlast the present age of the universe.

blocks.html: Light carries momentum, as you saw in energy and momentum of light: a flux $F$ presses on what absorbs or scatters it with a force $F/c$ per unit area of target. In a very luminous star the outflowing light pushes on the gas hard enough to compete with gravity. That sets the most luminous a star of a given mass can be, and it explains why the mass–luminosity relation cannot climb forever.

In ionized hydrogen, light scatters off free electrons, each presenting a target area $\sigma_T = 6.65 \times 10^{-29}$ m². At distance $r$ the flux is $L/(4\pi r^2)$, so the push on one electron is $\sigma_TL/(4\pi r^2c)$. The electrons cannot leave the protons behind (their electric attraction is enormous), so the push on an electron must hold up a proton against gravity, $GMm_p/r^2$. Setting the two equal, $r^2$ cancels: $$L_{\text{Edd}} = \frac{4\pi GMm_pc}{\sigma_T}.$$ Above it, radiation would blow the outer layers away.

The Eddington luminosity is $L_{\text{Edd}} = 4\pi GMm_pc/\sigma_T \approx 1.3 \times 10^{31}\text{ W} \times (M/M_\odot)$, about $3.3 \times 10^{4}\,L_\odot$ per solar mass. It is the same at every radius, and it applies to anything shining by its own light while held by gravity, from stars to the gas falling into black holes.

blocks.name: ph-star
blocks.cap: Radiation pressure against gravity on a parcel of gas. For the most massive stars, the luminosity on the main sequence approaches the Eddington limit.

blocks.title: The Sun's limit
blocks.q: Evaluate $L_{\text{Edd}}$ for $1\,M_\odot$.
blocks.a: About $3.3 \times 10^{4}\,L_\odot$. The Sun shines at only $3 \times 10^{-5}$ of its limit.

blocks.title: A very massive star
blocks.q: A $60\,M_\odot$ star following $L \approx 1.4\,M^{3.5}$ would have $L \approx 2.3 \times 10^{6}\,L_\odot$. Compare with its Eddington limit.
blocks.a: It would exceed the limit, so real stars this massive cannot follow the steep relation; their luminosity rises only about in proportion to $M$, and they drive powerful winds.

blocks.title: Weighing a quasar
blocks.q: A quasar shines with $1.0 \times 10^{40}$ W. If it is at or below its Eddington limit, what is the least its black hole can weigh?
blocks.a: At least about $8 \times 10^{8}\,M_\odot$.

blocks.html: Thinking a star can be as luminous as it likes, whatever its mass. Light pushes on matter, and that push grows with luminosity while gravity grows with mass. At $L_{\text{Edd}}$ they balance, so a star of mass $M$ cannot shine much above $3.3 \times 10^{4}\,(M/M_\odot)\,L_\odot$ and stay intact. That is one reason the most massive stars known, in the R136 cluster of the Large Magellanic Cloud, have on the order of 200 solar masses and not thousands. Check: radiation force over gravity is $L/L_{\text{Edd}}$, independent of distance.

blocks.html: The proton–proton chain makes two electron neutrinos for every helium nucleus. Neutrinos (see leptons, hadrons and quarks) feel only the weak force, so almost every one of them flies straight out of the Sun, and straight through Earth.

Light from the core needs on the order of $10^{5}$ years to random-walk out. Neutrinos cross the Sun in about 2 seconds and reach us about 8 minutes after they are made. So they show what fusion in the core is doing now. Their number follows from the luminosity: two neutrinos per 26.7 MeV, so $$\dot N_\nu = \frac{2L_\odot}{26.7\text{ MeV}} = \frac{2(3.83 \times 10^{26}\text{ W})}{4.28 \times 10^{-12}\text{ J}},$$ about $1.8 \times 10^{38}$ neutrinos per second.

About $6.4 \times 10^{14}$ solar neutrinos cross every square meter at Earth each second (about $6 \times 10^{10}$ per cm²), day and night. Detectors catch only a handful. The solar neutrino problem, that experiments found too few electron neutrinos, was solved by neutrino oscillations: neutrinos change flavor on the way, which means they have mass.

items: From the late 1960s, Raymond Davis's chlorine tank deep in the Homestake mine in South Dakota counted only about a third of the predicted electron neutrinos.
Either the solar models or our understanding of neutrinos had to be wrong. Helioseismology kept confirming the models.
Super-Kamiokande in Japan reported neutrino oscillations in 1998, and in 2001–2002 the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory in Canada measured all three flavors together: the total matched the solar models.
The work earned Nobel Prizes in 2002 (Davis and Masatoshi Koshiba) and 2015 (Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald).

blocks.q: How many solar neutrinos pass through 1 cm² each second at Earth?
steps: Flux: $1.8 \times 10^{38}/(4\pi(1.496 \times 10^{11}\text{ m})^2) = 6.4 \times 10^{14}$ per m² per second.
blocks.a: About $6 \times 10^{10}$ per second, some 60 billion, without effect.

blocks.title: News from the core
blocks.q: How long after they are made do the neutrinos reach Earth?
steps: They cross the Sun at nearly $c$ in about 2.3 s, then travel $1.496 \times 10^{11}$ m.
blocks.a: About 8.3 minutes, so a neutrino detector watches the core in close to real time.

blocks.html: Thinking neutrinos are blocked by the Sun's layers, like light. Light interacts with charged particles constantly and random-walks out over a long time. Neutrinos interact only through the weak force; a neutrino of solar energy would typically pass through light-years of lead before stopping. Check: solar neutrino detectors work the same at night, with all of Earth between them and the Sun.

blocks.html: A star spends most of its life on the main sequence, slowly turning hydrogen into helium in its core. In Red Giants and White Dwarfs you saw what comes next. Here we follow the path, or evolutionary track, a star traces on the H–R diagram, and connect each turn to what is happening in its core. The tool is the one from effective temperature and radius: $L = 4\pi R^2\sigma T^4$, so a move to the right at the same luminosity means the star is swelling.

The core drives everything. While hydrogen burns in the core, a star changes slowly: helium builds up, the core contracts a little and heats, and the luminosity creeps up (the young Sun gave out only about 70% of its present power). When core hydrogen runs out, nothing balances the core's energy loss, so it contracts and heats, as the virial theorem requires. Hydrogen keeps burning in a shell around it, and the extra energy from the shell inflates the envelope, which cools. The star moves right, then up the red-giant branch. When the core reaches about 100 million K, helium fuses to carbon and oxygen, the star settles down for a while, and the cycle repeats with the next fuel.

Stars do not move along the main sequence as they age; they sit near one point on it and then leave it. A Sun-like star goes: main sequence → subgiant → red giant → helium burning (horizontal branch or red clump) → asymptotic giant branch → planetary nebula → white dwarf. Massive stars cross the diagram almost horizontally, at nearly constant luminosity, becoming red supergiants.

blocks.cap: Evolutionary tracks for stars of 1, 5 and 15 solar masses. Each starts on the main sequence and leaves it to the upper right; the massive ones cross nearly horizontally.

blocks.title: How much does a red giant swell?
blocks.q: A star leaves the main sequence at $L = 1.0\,L_\odot$, $T = 5800$ K and later sits at $L = 100\,L_\odot$, $T = 4200$ K. By what factor has its radius grown?
blocks.a: About 19 times larger.

blocks.title: The Sun at the tip of the red-giant branch
blocks.q: Near the top of its red-giant branch the Sun will reach about $2500\,L_\odot$ at about 3000 K. What will its radius be, in AU?
blocks.a: About 0.86 AU, past the orbits of Mercury and Venus. (Whether it reaches Earth depends on how much mass the Sun loses first.)

blocks.title: Dating a cluster from its turnoff
blocks.q: The brightest main-sequence stars left in a cluster have about $100\,L_\odot$. Using $L \propto M^{3.5}$ and a lifetime of $10\text{ Gyr} \times M^{-2.5}$, how old is the cluster?
blocks.a: About 400 million years. All stars in a cluster formed together, so the stars just leaving the main sequence tell its age.

blocks.html: Thinking stars move along the main sequence as they age, sliding from hot to cool. The main sequence is a sequence of mass: each star lands at the point set by its mass and stays near it for 90% of its life, brightening slowly. When it ages it leaves the main sequence for the giant region. Check: a 1 $M_\odot$ star never becomes a red dwarf, and a cluster's main sequence gets shorter from the top as it ages, it does not shift.

When the core of a Sun-like star starts burning helium, its electrons are degenerate (see the next topic), so the ignition runs away almost at once: the helium flash. Stars above about 2 solar masses ignite helium gently.

blocks.html: What holds up a white dwarf? Not heat: it has no fusion and slowly cools forever. The answer is quantum mechanics, the same exclusion principle that builds the periodic table, applied to the electrons squeezed together in its dense matter.

The exclusion principle allows only two electrons (spin up and spin down) in each quantum state. Squeeze $n_e$ electrons per cubic meter into a box and the states fill up from the lowest momentum: the uncertainty principle says an electron confined to a spacing $\Delta x \sim n_e^{-1/3}$ must have momentum $p \sim \hbar n_e^{1/3}$. Counting states exactly, every state up to the Fermi momentum $p_F = \hbar(3\pi^2n_e)^{1/3}$ is filled, even at zero temperature. Pressure is momentum flux, roughly $n_e \times p \times v$ with $v = p/m_e$, so $$P \sim \frac{n_e\,p_F^2}{m_e} \propto \frac{\hbar^2n_e^{5/3}}{m_e}, \qquad \text{exactly } P = \frac{(3\pi^2)^{2/3}\hbar^2}{5m_e}\,n_e^{5/3}.$$ Electrons dominate rather than protons because the pressure goes as $1/m$: at the same momentum, the light electrons move about 1,800 times faster.

Electron degeneracy pressure comes from the exclusion principle, not from heat. It grows as $n_e^{5/3}$ and does not depend on temperature. Matter is degenerate when the Fermi energy $p_F^2/(2m_e)$ is much larger than $kT$.

blocks.name: ph-quantum
blocks.cap: Electrons filling the lowest energy levels, two per level. Even with no heat at all, the top ones (at the Fermi energy) move fast and push back when squeezed.

blocks.title: Electrons in white-dwarf matter
blocks.q: Carbon–oxygen matter at $1.0 \times 10^{9}$ kg/m³ has $\mu_e = 2$ nucleons per electron. Find $n_e$ and $p_F$.
blocks.a: $p_F \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-22}$ kg·m/s, about $0.8\,m_ec$: the fastest electrons move at a large fraction of the speed of light.

blocks.title: Degenerate versus thermal pressure
blocks.q: Compare the degeneracy pressure at that density with the ideal-gas pressure $n_ekT$ at $T = 10^{7}$ K.
blocks.a: The degeneracy pressure is about 75 times larger. Equivalently, $E_F \approx 160$ keV against $kT \approx 0.9$ keV.

blocks.title: Squeezing harder
blocks.q: If white-dwarf matter is compressed to 8 times its density, how does the (nonrelativistic) degeneracy pressure change?
blocks.a: 32 times larger, with no change in temperature.

blocks.html: Thinking a white dwarf is held up by hot gas pressure. A white dwarf has no energy source; it radiates away its heat and cools for billions of years, yet it does not shrink, because its support does not depend on temperature. The pressure comes from electrons forced into high-momentum states by the exclusion principle. Check with numbers: $E_F$ is hundreds of times $kT$ inside, so cooling barely changes the pressure.

blocks.html: White dwarfs behave in a way that surprises everyone the first time: the more massive a white dwarf, the smaller it is. It follows from combining degeneracy pressure with what hydrostatic equilibrium demands. A typical white dwarf holds about 0.6 solar masses in a ball about the size of Earth (that is how a Sun-like star ends).

Gravity needs a central pressure $P_c \sim GM^2/R^4$. Degeneracy supplies $P \propto n_e^{5/3} \propto \rho^{5/3} \propto (M/R^3)^{5/3} = M^{5/3}/R^5$. Setting them proportional: $$\frac{M^{5/3}}{R^5} \propto \frac{M^2}{R^4} \quad\Rightarrow\quad R \propto M^{-1/3}.$$ Adding mass makes gravity's demand grow faster than the supply at the old size, so the star must shrink until the denser electrons push back hard enough. Another way to say it: $MR^3$ is the same for all such white dwarfs, so volume goes as $1/M$.

For white dwarfs, $R \propto M^{-1/3}$: heavier ones are smaller and much denser ($\bar\rho \propto M/R^3 \propto M^2$). A $0.6\,M_\odot$ white dwarf has $R \approx 8{,}700$ km and a mean density near $4 \times 10^{8}$ kg/m³.

blocks.name: astrophys-plot
blocks.cap: Radius against mass for white dwarfs. Solid: the simple $R \propto M^{-1/3}$ law. Dashed: a fit that includes relativistic electrons (Nauenberg 1972), which drops to zero at about $1.44\,M_\odot$. Dots: two measured white dwarfs. Drag the mass to read off sizes and densities.

blocks.title: A heavier white dwarf
blocks.q: A $0.6\,M_\odot$ white dwarf has $R = 8700$ km. Estimate the radius of a $1.0\,M_\odot$ white dwarf with $R \propto M^{-1/3}$.
blocks.a: About 7,300 km. Real ones are smaller still (Sirius B: about 5,800 km), because near this mass relativity softens the electrons' pressure.

blocks.title: A teaspoon of white dwarf
blocks.q: Find the mean density of a $0.6\,M_\odot$, 8,700 km white dwarf and the mass of 5 cm³ of it.
blocks.a: A teaspoon would hold about 2,200 kg, the mass of a large car.

blocks.title: The exponent for a general law
blocks.q: If $P \propto \rho^{\gamma}$, what power $x$ appears in $R \propto M^{x}$?
blocks.a: $x = -1/3$ for nonrelativistic electrons. At $\gamma = 4/3$ the denominator is zero, a warning sign that the next topic explains.

blocks.html: Thinking more massive white dwarfs must be bigger, as for planets made of ordinary rock. Ordinary matter resists compression almost regardless of the load, so adding mass adds volume. Degenerate matter is soft by comparison: extra mass squeezes all of it. Check: Sirius B ($1.0\,M_\odot$) is smaller than Earth, while 40 Eridani B ($0.57\,M_\odot$) is larger.

blocks.html: In 1930, on a ship from India to England, the 19-year-old Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar added special relativity to the theory of white-dwarf sizes and found that there is a largest possible white dwarf. The result earned him a share of the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics.

As a white dwarf gains mass and shrinks, its electrons are squeezed to higher momenta. Once $p_F \gtrsim m_ec$, the fastest electrons move at nearly $c$ instead of $p/m_e$. The pressure, roughly $n_e \times p_F \times v$, then grows as $n_e \times n_e^{1/3} \times c$, so $P \propto \rho^{4/3}$ instead of $\rho^{5/3}$. Compare with gravity: $P \propto (M/R^3)^{4/3} = M^{4/3}/R^4$, while gravity needs $M^2/R^4$. Both go as $1/R^4$, so shrinking no longer helps. Only one mass balances; above it, gravity wins at every radius and the star collapses. Dimensional analysis gives that mass from the constants alone: $$M \sim \left(\frac{\hbar c}{G}\right)^{3/2}\frac{1}{(\mu_em_p)^2} \approx 0.5\,M_\odot \text{ for } \mu_e = 2,$$ and the full calculation multiplies it by about 3.1.

The Chandrasekhar limit is $M_{\text{Ch}} \approx 5.83\,M_\odot/\mu_e^2$, about $1.4\,M_\odot$ for carbon, oxygen or helium ($\mu_e = 2$). No white dwarf, and no stellar core supported by electron degeneracy, can be heavier.

blocks.title: The dimensional estimate
blocks.q: Evaluate $(\hbar c/G)^{3/2}/(\mu_em_p)^2$ for $\mu_e = 2$ ($\hbar c = 3.16 \times 10^{-26}$ J·m).
steps: $(2m_p)^2 = 1.12 \times 10^{-53}$ kg², so the ratio is $9.2 \times 10^{29}$ kg.
blocks.a: About $0.46\,M_\odot$; times 3.1 gives about $1.4\,M_\odot$.

blocks.title: When do the electrons become relativistic?
blocks.q: At what density does $p_F = m_ec$ for $\mu_e = 2$?
blocks.a: About $2 \times 10^{9}$ kg/m³, a few times the mean density of a typical white dwarf and about its central density. In heavier white dwarfs, the central electrons are strongly relativistic.

blocks.title: An iron core
blocks.q: What is the limit for a core of iron-56 ($Z = 26$)?
blocks.a: About $1.26\,M_\odot$ in this simple model: iron has fewer electrons per nucleon, so it can support less.

blocks.html: Applying the limit to the whole star. A star of 6 solar masses can still end as a white dwarf: it sheds most of its mass in winds and a planetary nebula, and only its core, below the limit, remains. The limit concerns the mass supported by degenerate electrons: a white dwarf, or the core inside a massive star. When a massive star's iron core grows past it, the core collapses (next topic). A white dwarf in a binary that gains matter until it nears the limit can explode as a type Ia supernova.

The 5.83 comes from solving the structure equations exactly for fully relativistic electrons. Detailed models with the electrons' finite mass and other small effects give about $1.4\,M_\odot$ for carbon–oxygen white dwarfs, and no white dwarf heavier than that has been found.

blocks.html: A star of more than about 8 solar masses fuses heavier and heavier elements in its core: hydrogen, helium, carbon, neon, oxygen, silicon. The last step builds iron and nickel, at the peak of the binding-energy curve, where fusion stops paying. An iron core grows until it passes the Chandrasekhar limit, and then it falls in on itself. You saw the outline in Supernovae and the Elements; here are the numbers.

Two processes rob the core of the electrons' support. Electrons are captured by protons ($p + e^- \to n + \nu_e$), and energetic photons break iron nuclei apart, which absorbs energy. Pressure falls, and the core collapses almost freely: a body falling under its own gravity takes about $t_{ff} = \sqrt{3\pi/(32G\bar\rho)}$, under a second at these densities, and the inner core's infall reaches about a quarter of the speed of light. It stops when it reaches nuclear density, at a radius of about 10 to 20 km, as a proto-neutron star. The gravitational energy released is about $$\tfrac35\frac{GM^2}{R} \approx \tfrac35\frac{(6.67 \times 10^{-11})(2.8 \times 10^{30})^2}{1.2 \times 10^{4}} \approx 3 \times 10^{46}\text{ J}.$$

A core-collapse supernova releases about $3 \times 10^{46}$ J. About 99% leaves as neutrinos within about ten seconds, about 1% becomes the kinetic energy of the exploding envelope, and only about 0.01% emerges as light, still enough to outshine a galaxy for weeks.

blocks.name: ph-nucleus
blocks.cap: Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron and nickel. Fusing up to the peak releases energy; going past it costs energy, so an iron core has no fuel left.

blocks.title: The collapse time
blocks.q: An iron core of $1.4\,M_\odot$ and radius 3,000 km loses its pressure support. Estimate its free-fall time.
blocks.a: About 0.4 s.

blocks.title: The energy budget
blocks.q: Estimate $\tfrac35GM^2/R$ for a $1.4\,M_\odot$ core that ends as a 12 km neutron star.
blocks.a: About $2.6 \times 10^{46}$ J, about 200 times the Sun's output over its whole 10-billion-year life.

blocks.title: Neutrinos from Supernova 1987A
blocks.q: In 1987 a star in the Large Magellanic Cloud (about 50 kpc away) exploded. If $3 \times 10^{46}$ J went into neutrinos of about 12 MeV each, how many crossed each cm² at Earth?
blocks.a: About $5 \times 10^{10}$ per cm². Detectors in Japan, the United States and Russia caught about two dozen of them, a few hours before the light was first seen.

blocks.html: Thinking most of a supernova's energy leaves as light. The light is spectacular, but it is roughly one part in ten thousand of the total. Almost all of the energy is carried off by neutrinos, which escape the dense core within seconds; the 1987A neutrinos arrived before the light because the light had to wait for the shock to reach the star's surface. Check the budget: about $10^{42}$ J of light against a few times $10^{46}$ J in all.
