blocks.html: The collapsed core of a core-collapse supernova becomes a ball of neutrons with a radius of only about 12 km, holding more mass than the Sun. In 1967 Jocelyn Bell Burnell, a graduate student at Cambridge, found radio pulses repeating every 1.337 seconds with clock-like precision; they turned out to come from spinning neutron stars, now called pulsars. Two conservation laws explain why they spin so fast and carry such strong magnetic fields.

Angular momentum. As in conservation of angular momentum, $I\omega$ stays the same when nothing twists the collapsing core. With $I \propto MR^2$, $R^2/P$ is conserved: shrinking the radius by a factor of 500 shortens the period by $500^2 = 250{,}000$. Magnetic flux. The core's hot plasma conducts electricity so well that the magnetic field lines are carried along with it, so the flux $\Phi \propto BR^2$ is conserved and $B$ grows by the same factor $R_i^2/R_f^2$.

Collapse conserves angular momentum ($P \propto R^2$) and magnetic flux ($B \propto 1/R^2$). So neutron stars spin with periods from about a millisecond to seconds and have fields around $10^{8}$ T (magnetars up to about $10^{11}$ T), against about $10^{-4}$ T at the Sun's surface. Their density, about $4 \times 10^{17}$ kg/m³, matches that of atomic nuclei.

blocks.name: ph-rotation
blocks.cap: The same physics as a spinning skater who pulls in her arms: a smaller moment of inertia means a faster spin.

blocks.title: Spinning up
blocks.q: A core of radius 6,000 km turns once every 30 minutes. It collapses to a 12 km neutron star. What is the new period?
blocks.a: $P_f = 7.2 \times 10^{-3}$ s: about 140 turns per second.

blocks.title: A teaspoon of neutron star
blocks.q: Find the mean density of a $1.4\,M_\odot$ neutron star of radius 12 km, and the mass of 5 cm³ of it.
blocks.a: A teaspoon would hold about $2 \times 10^{12}$ kg, some 2 billion tonnes.

blocks.title: How fast can it spin?
blocks.q: The equator of a spinning star must not move faster than orbital speed. What is the shortest period for $1.4\,M_\odot$ and $R = 12$ km?
blocks.a: $P_{\min} \approx 0.6$ ms. The fastest known pulsar turns 716 times a second (1.4 ms); a white dwarf could never spin that fast without flying apart.

blocks.html: Thinking a neutron star spins slowly because the star it came from did. The Sun takes almost a month to turn, but shrink it to 12 km and conservation of angular momentum would spin it up by a factor of about $(7 \times 10^{5}/12)^2 \approx 3 \times 10^{9}$. Real cores lose some angular momentum along the way, yet young pulsars still spin many times a second. Check: $P \propto R^2$, so a large shrink means a huge spin-up.

blocks.html: A pulsar shines like a lighthouse: its strong magnetic field channels beams of radiation out from the magnetic poles, and if the magnetic axis is tilted from the spin axis, the beams sweep around. Each time one crosses Earth we see a pulse. The neutron star is not burning anything; it shines by spending its rotational energy, and we can watch it slow down. The tool is rotational work and power.

A spinning body stores $E = \tfrac12I\omega^2$, with $\omega = 2\pi/P$, so $E = 2\pi^2I/P^2$. Differentiate with respect to time: $$\frac{dE}{dt} = I\omega\dot\omega = -\frac{4\pi^2I\dot P}{P^3}.$$ Pulsar timing measures $P$ and its tiny rate of increase $\dot P$ with great precision, and $I \approx 10^{38}$ kg·m² for a neutron star of 1.4 solar masses and about 10 km. If the pulsar has slowed down steadily from a much faster spin, its age is about $\tau = P/(2\dot P)$.
Spin-down power $|\dot E| = 4\pi^2I\dot P/P^3$; characteristic age $\tau = P/(2\dot P)$. A young pulsar loses rotational energy fast enough to power the nebula of glowing gas and particles around it.

blocks.cap: A neutron star whose magnetic axis is tilted from its spin axis. Each beam sweeps around once per turn; we see a pulse when one crosses our line of sight.

blocks.title: The Crab pulsar's energy store
blocks.q: The Crab pulsar has $P = 0.0337$ s and $I = 1.0 \times 10^{38}$ kg·m². How much rotational energy does it have?
blocks.a: About $1.7 \times 10^{42}$ J.

blocks.title: Its spin-down power
blocks.q: The Crab's period grows at $\dot P = 4.2 \times 10^{-13}$ s per second. Find $|\dot E|$.
blocks.a: About $4.3 \times 10^{31}$ W, about 100,000 times the Sun's luminosity. The Crab Nebula radiates roughly $10^{31}$ W across the spectrum, about a quarter of that.

blocks.title: Its age
blocks.q: Estimate the Crab pulsar's characteristic age.
blocks.a: About 1,300 years. Chinese astronomers recorded the supernova in 1054, about 970 years ago: close. The formula assumes the pulsar started out spinning much faster than it does now; the difference tells us the Crab was born with a period not far below today's.

blocks.html: Thinking a pulsar shines because it is still hot from the explosion. Its surface is hot, but its thermal glow is far too weak to supply the power we measure. Young pulsars and their nebulae are powered by rotation: the star is a flywheel being slowed down by its magnetic field, and the lost rotational energy, $4\pi^2I\dot P/P^3$, matches what the nebula radiates. Check: the Crab's spin-down power is a few times the nebula's output, as it must be.

blocks.html: In 1783 John Michell asked what would happen if a star were so compact that its escape speed exceeded the speed of light. Using escape speed, $v = \sqrt{2GM/r}$, the answer is easy to find. In 1916 Karl Schwarzschild found the same radius in Einstein's general relativity, where it marks the event horizon of a black hole (see Black Holes).

Set the escape speed equal to $c$: $\sqrt{2GM/r} = c$ gives $r = 2GM/c^2$. Newton's reasoning lands on the right formula partly by luck; in general relativity the horizon is where even outward-moving light can no longer get farther from the center, and nothing that crosses it comes back. The radius is proportional to the mass: $2G M_\odot/c^2 = 2.95$ km.
The Schwarzschild radius is $$r_s = \frac{2GM}{c^2} \approx 2.95\text{ km} \times \frac{M}{M_\odot}.$$ Outside a black hole, far from the horizon, its gravity is just $GM/r^2$, like any other mass.

blocks.title: A stellar black hole
blocks.q: Find $r_s$ for $10\,M_\odot$.
blocks.a: About 29.5 km, the size of a city.

blocks.title: How dense is a black hole?
blocks.q: Find the mean density inside the horizon of a $10^{9}\,M_\odot$ black hole.
blocks.a: About 18 kg/m³, less dense than water. Since $r_s \propto M$, mean density falls as $1/M^2$; a solar-mass black hole averages about $2 \times 10^{19}$ kg/m³.

blocks.title: The Sun as a black hole
blocks.q: If the Sun were squeezed into a black hole of the same mass, what would happen to Earth's orbit?
steps: Outside a spherical mass, gravity is $GM/r^2$, whatever the size (the shell theorem).
blocks.a: Earth would keep orbiting exactly as before, only in the dark.

blocks.html: Thinking a black hole pulls harder than the star that formed it, at the same distance. A black hole is not a cosmic vacuum cleaner. Its gravity is extreme only because you can get very close to all of its mass; at 1 AU a 10-solar-mass black hole pulls exactly like a 10-solar-mass star. Check with $g = GM/r^2$: it contains no radius of the object, only the distance to its center.

blocks.html: Near a mass, clocks run slow and light loses energy as it climbs out. This is a second, separate kind of time dilation from the one in special relativity, which comes from motion. It is set by the Schwarzschild radius and by how close you are to it.

A photon of energy $E = hf$ carries mass-equivalent $E/c^2$. Climbing out of a gravitational well from radius $R$ to far away costs it about $(E/c^2)(GM/R)$, so its frequency drops by a fraction $$\frac{\Delta f}{f} \approx \frac{GM}{Rc^2}.$$ Equivalently, a clock deep in the well ticks slower than one far away. In general relativity the exact rate for a clock hovering at radius $r$ outside a nonspinning mass is $$\frac{d\tau}{dt} = \sqrt{1 - \frac{r_s}{r}},$$ which reduces to $1 - GM/(rc^2)$ when $r \gg r_s$.

Light leaving radius $r$ arrives far away stretched by $1 + z = 1/\sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$ (so $z \approx GM/(rc^2)$ in a weak field). At the horizon the factor becomes infinite. This effect depends on where a clock is; special relativity's time dilation depends on how fast it moves.

blocks.cap: Clocks at different distances from a black hole (in units of $r_s$). Clocks closer in tick more slowly as seen from far away.

blocks.title: Sirius B's redshift
blocks.q: Sirius B has $1.02\,M_\odot$ and $R = 5{,}840$ km. Find $GM/(Rc^2)$ and the equivalent Doppler speed $cz$.
blocks.a: About 77 km/s; measurements of Sirius B's spectral lines give about 80 km/s. (For the Sun the shift is only 0.64 km/s.)

blocks.title: GPS clocks
blocks.q: GPS satellites orbit at $r = 2.66 \times 10^{7}$ m. How much faster does gravity make their clocks run than ground clocks, per day? ($GM_\oplus = 3.99 \times 10^{14}$ m³/s².)
blocks.a: About 45.7 μs per day fast. Their orbital speed slows them by about 7.2 μs per day (special relativity), so the net is about 38.5 μs per day, which the system corrects for.

blocks.title: Near a black hole
blocks.q: A clock hovers at $r = 2r_s$. How long does a distant observer see it take to tick off 1 hour?
blocks.a: About 1.41 hours; its light arrives with wavelengths stretched by the same factor 1.41.

blocks.html: Mixing up gravitational time dilation with the time dilation of motion. Special relativity's $\gamma$ depends on speed and is symmetric (each observer sees the other's clock slow). Gravitational time dilation depends on position in a gravitational field and is not symmetric: the clock lower in the well runs slow as judged by both. GPS needs both effects, and they have opposite signs. Check the sign: a higher clock always runs fast compared with a lower one.
In 1960 Robert Pound and Glen Rebka reported measuring the shift for gamma rays climbing a 22.5 m tower at Harvard: $\Delta f/f = gh/c^2 = 2.5 \times 10^{-15}$, as predicted.

blocks.html: Gravity weakens with distance, so the near side of a body is pulled harder than its far side. That difference, the tidal force, stretches the body along the line to the other mass. It raises ocean tides, it tears apart moons that stray too close, and near a small black hole it would pull you apart. The tool is linear approximation applied to gravity outside a sphere.

The acceleration toward a mass $M$ is $a(r) = GM/r^2$. Two points separated by a small $\Delta r$ along the line to $M$ feel accelerations that differ by about $$\Delta a \approx \left|\frac{da}{dr}\right|\Delta r = \frac{2GM}{r^3}\,\Delta r.$$ The derivative of $1/r^2$ is $-2/r^3$, so the tidal effect falls off one power faster than gravity itself. In the frame of the body's center, the near side is pulled toward $M$ and the far side is left behind: two bulges, not one.
Tidal acceleration across a length $\Delta r$ at distance $r$: $\Delta a \approx 2GM\,\Delta r/r^3$. It goes as $M/r^3$, so a near, small body (the Moon) can out-tide a far, huge one (the Sun).

blocks.cap: The difference between the Moon's pull on each part of Earth and its pull on Earth's center. The arrows point away from Earth on both the near and far sides: two tidal bulges.

blocks.title: The Moon and the Sun on Earth's oceans
blocks.q: Compare the tidal accelerations from the Moon ($7.35 \times 10^{22}$ kg at $3.84 \times 10^{8}$ m) and the Sun ($1.99 \times 10^{30}$ kg at $1.50 \times 10^{11}$ m) across Earth's radius ($6.37 \times 10^{6}$ m).
steps: Sun: $5.0 \times 10^{-7}$ m/s², so the Sun's tidal effect is about $0.45$ of the Moon's.
blocks.a: The Moon raises tides about twice as strong as the Sun's, even though the Sun pulls Earth about 180 times harder.

blocks.title: The Roche limit
blocks.q: A rock sits on the near side of a moon of radius $r$ and density $\rho_m$ orbiting a planet of radius $R_P$ and density $\rho_P$ at distance $d$. Where does the planet's tidal pull beat the moon's own gravity?
steps: Self-gravity: $Gm/r^2$ with $m = \tfrac43\pi r^3\rho_m$. Tidal pull: $2GM\,r/d^3$ with $M = \tfrac43\pi R_P^3\rho_P$.
blocks.a: For icy bodies ($900$ kg/m³) near Saturn ($R_P = 60{,}300$ km, $687$ kg/m³) that is about 69,000 km; a fluid moon breaks up farther out, near $2.44R_P(\rho_P/\rho_m)^{1/3} \approx 135{,}000$ km. Saturn's bright main rings lie roughly inside that distance.

blocks.title: Falling into a black hole
blocks.q: Find the tidal difference across a 2 m body at the horizon of a $10\,M_\odot$ black hole ($r_s = 2.95 \times 10^{4}$ m).
blocks.a: About 20 million $g$: fatal "spaghettification" well outside the horizon. At the horizon of Sagittarius A* ($4.3 \times 10^{6}\,M_\odot$) the same difference is only $10^{-3}$ m/s², since $\Delta a$ at $r_s$ goes as $1/M^2$.

blocks.html: Thinking tidal force falls off as $1/r^2$, like gravity itself. It is a difference of gravity across a body, and the difference falls off as $1/r^3$: double the distance and gravity drops to a quarter, but tides drop to an eighth. Check: if tides went as $M/r^2$, the Sun's tides would be 180 times the Moon's instead of about half.
In 1992 comet Shoemaker–Levy 9 passed inside Jupiter's Roche limit and was torn into more than 20 pieces, which struck Jupiter in July 1994.

blocks.html: When gas falls onto a compact object, it speeds up enormously, and when it is stopped or swirls into a disk, that energy turns into heat and light. In X-ray binaries a neutron star or a black hole pulls gas off a companion star; around supermassive black holes, accretion powers quasars. How much energy can falling release?

A kilogram falling from far away to the surface of a body of mass $M$ and radius $R$ loses potential energy $GM/R$ (with $U = 0$ at infinity). If that energy is radiated, a stream of $\dot m$ kilograms per second gives $$L_{\text{acc}} = \frac{GM\dot m}{R}.$$ Compare with rest energy: falling releases a fraction $GM/(Rc^2)$ of $mc^2$. For fusion of hydrogen into helium the fraction is 0.007. For a neutron star it is about 0.15 to 0.2.

Accretion releases $GM/R$ per kilogram, a fraction $\eta \approx GM/(Rc^2)$ of the rest energy. The more compact the object, the larger $\eta$: about $10^{-4}$ for a white dwarf, about 0.15 to 0.2 for a neutron star, and about 0.06 to 0.4 for gas spiraling into a black hole (depending on its spin), compared with 0.007 for hydrogen fusion.

blocks.q: How much energy does each kilogram release falling onto a $1.4\,M_\odot$ neutron star of radius 12 km? Compare with fusion.
blocks.a: About 25 times more than fusing the same kilogram of hydrogen.

blocks.title: An X-ray binary
blocks.q: Gas lands on that neutron star at $10^{14}$ kg/s. How luminous is it?

blocks.title: Feeding a quasar
blocks.q: A quasar shines with $10^{40}$ W at an efficiency $\eta = 0.1$. How much mass does its black hole swallow per year?
blocks.a: About 18 solar masses per year.

blocks.html: Thinking fusion always releases more energy per kilogram than falling. Fusion beats falling onto ordinary stars and white dwarfs, but near a neutron star or black hole, gravity wins by a wide margin: a kilogram dropped onto a neutron star releases more energy than fusing it would, about 25 times more. That is why the brightest steady X-ray sources in the sky, such as Scorpius X-1, are accreting neutron stars and black holes. Check: compare $GM/(Rc^2)$ with 0.007.

blocks.html: Einstein's general relativity predicts that moving masses send out ripples in spacetime itself, traveling at the speed of light. They are produced most strongly by pairs of compact objects, such as the black holes and neutron stars of this unit, orbiting each other closely.

As two masses orbit, the pattern of their gravitational field swings around, and the changing curvature spreads outward as a wave. The pattern repeats every half orbit, when the two masses have swapped places, so the wave frequency is twice the orbital frequency. The waves carry away energy, so the orbit shrinks. A smaller orbit is faster, so the frequency and the strength of the waves both rise: the signal "chirps" up until the two objects merge. A passing wave stretches distances in one direction across its path while squeezing them in the perpendicular direction, by a fraction $h$ called the strain.

Gravitational waves are ripples of spacetime curvature, traveling at $c$, with $f_{\text{GW}} = 2f_{\text{orb}}$. A detector arm of length $L$ changes by $\Delta L = hL$; for real signals $h \sim 10^{-21}$.

items: 1916: Einstein predicts gravitational waves from general relativity.

1974: Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor discover a binary pulsar. Years of timing show its orbit shrinking at the rate the theory predicts for energy carried off by gravitational waves (Nobel Prize 1993).

September 14, 2015: the two LIGO detectors in the United States record waves from two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses merging about 1.3 billion light-years away; about 3 solar masses of energy left as gravitational waves (Nobel Prize 2017 to Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne).
August 17, 2017: LIGO and Virgo record two neutron stars merging about 40 Mpc away; gamma rays arrive 1.7 seconds later, and telescopes watch the glowing debris, rich in newly made heavy elements.

blocks.title: How small is the stretch?
blocks.q: A wave with $h = 1.0 \times 10^{-21}$ passes a LIGO arm 4.0 km long. By how much does the arm change?
blocks.a: $4.0 \times 10^{-18}$ m, a few thousandths of the width of a proton. LIGO bounces laser light back and forth to sense it.

blocks.title: The energy of a merger
blocks.q: About $3.0\,M_\odot$ of mass-energy left as gravitational waves in GW150914. How much energy is that?
blocks.a: About $5.4 \times 10^{47}$ J, released in a fraction of a second. At its peak, the merger's power was greater than the light output of all the stars in the observable universe combined.

blocks.title: Gravity travels at the speed of light
blocks.q: Gamma rays from the 2017 merger arrived 1.7 s after the gravitational waves, after a trip of about 40 Mpc. Bound the fractional difference in speed.
blocks.a: About $4 \times 10^{-16}$: the two travel at the same speed to within parts in $10^{15}$.

blocks.html: Thinking gravitational waves are sound waves in space, or the same as "gravity waves" in water and air. Sound needs a material to travel through and moves far slower than light. Gravity waves in fluids are ordinary water or air waves in which gravity is the restoring force. Gravitational waves are oscillations of spacetime itself: they need no medium, travel at $c$ through empty space, and stretch and squeeze everything they pass across their direction of travel. Check: LIGO measured them crossing about a billion light-years of nearly empty space.

blocks.html: How do you weigh a galaxy? The same way you weigh the Sun: watch something orbit it. In a spiral galaxy, stars and gas clouds circle the center, and Doppler shifts give their speeds at every radius. A plot of orbital speed against radius is a rotation curve. In Dark Matter you saw what it revealed; here you will do the calculation, using the shell theorem.

For a roughly spherical distribution of mass, a body orbiting at radius $r$ feels only the mass $M(r)$ inside its orbit, as if it were at the center. A circular orbit needs $v^2/r = GM(r)/r^2$, so $$v(r) = \sqrt{\frac{GM(r)}{r}}, \qquad M(r) = \frac{v^2r}{G}.$$ If nearly all of the mass sat in the bright center, $M(r)$ would stop growing beyond it and orbital speeds would fall as $1/\sqrt{r}$, like the planets. Instead, from the 1970s Vera Rubin and Kent Ford and later radio astronomers found that the curves of spiral galaxies stay flat far beyond the visible disk.

A flat rotation curve ($v$ constant) means $M(r) = v^2r/G$ keeps growing in proportion to $r$, out where there are few stars and little gas. Most of a galaxy's mass is invisible: dark matter, in a halo with density falling roughly as $1/r^2$.

blocks.name: ph-orbit
blocks.cap: Orbital speed against distance from the center. The dashed curve is what the visible stars and gas alone would produce; the measured curve stays flat.

blocks.title: Weighing the Milky Way inside the Sun's orbit
blocks.q: The Sun orbits the galactic center at about 230 km/s, 8.2 kpc out. How much mass lies inside the Sun's orbit, and how long is one orbit? ($1\text{ kpc} = 3.09 \times 10^{19}$ m.)
blocks.a: About $10^{11}\,M_\odot$, and one "galactic year" of about 220 million years.

blocks.title: What Kepler would predict
blocks.q: Stars 10 kpc out in a galaxy orbit at 220 km/s. If all the mass were inside 10 kpc, how fast would gas at 40 kpc orbit?
blocks.a: 110 km/s. Measured curves stay near 220 km/s instead, so the mass inside 40 kpc is four times the mass inside 10 kpc.

blocks.title: The dark halo's density
blocks.q: For a flat curve at 220 km/s, the density at radius $r$ is $\rho = v^2/(4\pi Gr^2)$. Evaluate it at 8 kpc.
steps: $\rho \approx 9 \times 10^{-22}$ kg/m³, or about $0.014\,M_\odot$ per cubic parsec.
blocks.a: A thin haze: roughly half a proton's mass per cubic centimeter, but spread through an enormous volume.

blocks.html: Missing why a flat curve is a surprise. With visible matter alone, the mass would be nearly all inside the bright inner disk, and stars and gas farther out should orbit more slowly, $v \propto 1/\sqrt{r}$, as the outer planets do. A flat curve means the enclosed mass keeps growing with radius even where we see almost nothing. Check with numbers: $M(r) = v^2r/G$ doubles from 10 kpc to 20 kpc when $v$ stays the same.

blocks.html: At the center of the Milky Way, in the constellation Sagittarius, sits a compact radio source called Sagittarius A*. For about 30 years, two teams led by Andrea Ghez and Reinhard Genzel followed individual stars as they whipped around it, using infrared light that passes through the dust. Their orbits are Kepler ellipses, and they weigh the central object exactly as visual binaries weigh stars. Its size is set by the Schwarzschild radius.

The star S2 has an orbital period of 16.0 years and an angular semi-major axis of $0.1255''$ at a distance of about 8.18 kpc. In AU, $a = 0.1255 \times 8180 \approx 1030$ AU. With Kepler's third law in solar units, $M = a^3/P^2 = 1030^3/16.0^2 \approx 4.2 \times 10^{6}\,M_\odot$. That much mass inside S2's closest approach, about 120 AU, can only be a black hole: no cluster of stars could be packed that tightly and survive.

The Milky Way's central black hole has about $4 \times 10^{6}$ solar masses. Most large galaxies have a central supermassive black hole, with masses up to billions of $M_\odot$, typically a few tenths of a percent of the mass of the galaxy's central bulge, and a tiny fraction of the whole galaxy.

blocks.name: astrophys-s2

opts.task: Play the orbit or drag the time: S2 spends years far out and whips past the black hole in a few months.

blocks.cap: S2's orbit around Sagittarius A*, to scale: a long ellipse with the black hole at one focus. The speeds come from the vis-viva equation for $4.2 \times 10^{6}\,M_\odot$.

blocks.title: Weighing Sagittarius A*
blocks.q: S2 has $a = 0.1255''$, $P = 16.0$ yr, and the galactic center is 8.18 kpc away. Find the black hole's mass.
blocks.a: About $4.2 \times 10^{6}\,M_\odot$. (Ghez and Genzel shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for this work, with Roger Penrose.)

blocks.title: How fast at closest approach?
blocks.q: S2's orbit has $a = 1030$ AU and $e = 0.886$. Find its speed at closest approach.
steps: $r_p = a(1 - e) = 117$ AU; angular momentum per mass $h = \sqrt{GMa(1 - e^2)}$, and $v_p = h/r_p$.
blocks.a: About 7,700 km/s, 2.6% of the speed of light. In 2018 astronomers measured S2's light reddened by gravity at that moment, as general relativity predicts.

blocks.title: How big does it look?
blocks.q: The black hole's shadow has a diameter of about $\sqrt{27}\,r_s$. For $4.3 \times 10^{6}\,M_\odot$ at 8.2 kpc, what angle does it span?
steps: $r_s = 2GM/c^2 = 1.27 \times 10^{10}$ m, so the shadow is $6.6 \times 10^{10}$ m across.
blocks.a: About 54 μas, like a doughnut on the Moon seen from Earth. The Event Horizon Telescope imaged a ring of about this size in 2022, after imaging M87's much larger black hole in 2019.

blocks.html: Thinking the central black hole holds most of a galaxy's mass. Four million solar masses is enormous for one object, but the Milky Way's stars alone total tens of billions of solar masses, and with dark matter the galaxy is near $10^{12}\,M_\odot$. The black hole is about 0.0004% of that. Its gravity dominates only within a few parsecs of the center. Check with the rotation curve: $v^2r/G$ at 8 kpc is $10^{11}\,M_\odot$, 25,000 times the black hole.

blocks.html: No single method measures every cosmic distance. Astronomers build a distance ladder: each rung uses a method that works over some range, calibrated by the rung below it where their ranges overlap. You met the standard candles; the distance modulus turns each one into a distance.

A standard candle is an object whose absolute magnitude $M$ we know; measure its apparent magnitude $m$ and $d = 10^{(m - M + 5)/5}$ pc. But to know $M$, you must first measure the distance to some examples by another method. Parallax, pure geometry, gives distances to nearby Cepheid variable stars (Gaia measures parallaxes for over a billion stars). Those Cepheids calibrate Henrietta Leavitt's period–luminosity relation (1912), so Cepheids in galaxies tens of megaparsecs away give those galaxies' distances. Type Ia supernovae that explode in those same galaxies calibrate the supernovae's peak brightness, about $M = -19.3$, and supernovae can be seen billions of light-years away.

Parallax → Cepheids → type Ia supernovae → Hubble's law. Each rung is only as good as the one beneath it: an error in a lower rung carries up into every distance above it, including the Hubble constant.

blocks.name: ph-cosmic
blocks.cap: The rungs of the distance ladder and the ranges where each works. Overlaps between rungs are where one calibrates the next.

blocks.name: ph-cosmic
blocks.cap: A Cepheid's brightness rises and falls with a regular period. The longer the period, the more luminous the star.

blocks.title: A Cepheid in a distant galaxy
blocks.q: A Cepheid pulsates every 30 days and has average apparent magnitude 25.0. Use $M_V = -2.43(\log_{10}P - 1) - 4.05$.
blocks.a: About 11 Mpc, roughly 36 million light-years.

blocks.title: A supernova much farther out
blocks.q: A type Ia supernova peaks at $m = 19.0$. With $M = -19.3$, how far away is it?
blocks.a: About 460 Mpc, roughly 1.5 billion light-years, far beyond the reach of Cepheids.

blocks.title: How errors climb the ladder
blocks.q: If the Cepheid calibration is off by 0.10 magnitude, how much are all the distances above it off?
steps: A magnitude error $\Delta$ is a distance factor $10^{\Delta/5} = 10^{0.02}$.
blocks.a: About 5% for every distance above, and 5% in the Hubble constant. That is why so much work goes into the lowest rungs.

blocks.html: Thinking one method measures distances all the way out. Parallax angles become too small to measure beyond a few thousand parsecs; individual Cepheids become too faint beyond about 40 Mpc; supernovae are rare and must be calibrated by Cepheids first. Every far distance therefore rests on all the rungs beneath it. Check any quoted distance by asking which method measured it, and what calibrated that method.

blocks.html: Edwin Hubble found that distant galaxies' spectra are shifted to the red, more so the farther away they are (see Hubble's Law). For nearby galaxies the shift looks like an ordinary Doppler shift. But in an expanding universe there is a cleaner way to think about it, and it is the one that works at any distance.

Describe the expansion with a scale factor $a(t)$: every distance between galaxies (far enough apart not to be bound together) is proportional to $a$, with $a = 1$ today. Light traveling between galaxies is stretched along with the space it crosses: each wave crest is carried apart with everything else. So if light left a galaxy when the scale factor was $a$ and arrives today, its wavelength has grown by $1/a$: $$1 + z = \frac{\lambda_{\text{obs}}}{\lambda_{\text{emit}}} = \frac{a_{\text{now}}}{a_{\text{then}}}.$$

A cosmological redshift tells you how much the universe has expanded while the light was on its way: $1 + z = 1/a$. A galaxy at $z = 1$ sent its light when distances were half of today's; the cosmic microwave background, at $z \approx 1100$, when they were about 1/1100 of today's.

blocks.name: ph-cosmic
blocks.cap: The scale factor against time, with a light wave stretching as the universe expands. At $z = 1$ the wavelength doubles.

blocks.name: ph-cosmic
blocks.cap: An expanding pattern of galaxies. Click any one: from every galaxy, all the others recede, faster the farther they are. There is no center.

blocks.title: A distant galaxy
blocks.q: The Lyman-alpha line (121.6 nm) of a galaxy is seen at 851 nm. Find $z$ and the scale factor when the light left.
blocks.a: $z = 6.0$: distances were one-seventh of today's. The line, emitted in the ultraviolet, now arrives as infrared light.

blocks.title: How much have distances grown?
blocks.q: Light from a quasar has $z = 3.0$. By what factor have distances between galaxies grown since it left?
blocks.a: Four times larger, so the average density of matter was $4^3 = 64$ times higher then.

blocks.title: Redshifts multiply
blocks.q: Light from a quasar at $z = 4$ passed a galaxy that we see at $z = 1$. What redshift did that galaxy see?
steps: Stretch factors multiply: $(1 + z_{\text{total}}) = (1 + z_1)(1 + z_2)$.
blocks.a: $z = 1.5$. Adding the redshifts (to get 3) would be wrong.

blocks.html: Thinking a cosmological redshift is only a Doppler shift from galaxies moving through space. For nearby galaxies the two pictures agree ($v \approx cz$). For distant ones the redshift measures the expansion of space during the trip, $1 + z = 1/a$, and plugging large $z$ into a Doppler formula gives a "speed" with no clear meaning. Distances between faraway galaxies can grow faster than $c$ without anything moving through space faster than light. Check: $1 + z$ is always a ratio of sizes of the universe.

blocks.html: For nearby galaxies the redshift and the distance are simply proportional: Hubble's law, $v = H_0d$. Running the expansion backward gives a first estimate of the age of the universe. Here is how to use the law well, and where it breaks.

The expansion rate is $H = \dot a/a$; today it is $H_0$. Two galaxies a distance $d$ apart move apart at $v = \dot a\,(d/a) = Hd$. For small $z$, the recession speed is $v \approx cz$, so $d \approx cz/H_0$. If galaxies had always moved apart at today's speeds, they would all have been together a time $d/v = 1/H_0$ ago: the Hubble time. With $H_0$ in km/s/Mpc, $$\frac{1}{H_0} = \frac{3.09 \times 10^{19}\text{ km}}{H_0\text{ km/s}} \approx \frac{978}{H_0}\text{ Gyr}.$$

For $z \ll 1$: $d \approx cz/H_0$. The Hubble time $1/H_0$ is about 14 Gyr for $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc. Measurements of $H_0$ range from about 67 (from the cosmic microwave background) to about 73 km/s/Mpc (from Cepheids and supernovae); why they differ is an open question.

blocks.name: ph-cosmic
blocks.cap: Recession speed against distance for galaxies. The slope is the Hubble constant; its inverse is the Hubble time.

blocks.title: A nearby galaxy
blocks.q: A galaxy has $z = 0.010$. With $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc, how far is it?
blocks.a: About 43 Mpc.

blocks.title: The Hubble time
blocks.q: Find $1/H_0$ for $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc.
blocks.a: About 14.0 Gyr, close to the age of 13.8 Gyr from detailed models: a coincidence of our era, as the next topics show.

blocks.title: Peculiar velocities
blocks.q: A galaxy recedes at 1,000 km/s, but 300 km/s of that is its own motion away from us within its group. How far is it, with $H_0 = 70$?
blocks.a: 10 Mpc; ignoring the peculiar velocity would give 14 Mpc, 40% too far. Far galaxies, with large $cz$, are hardly affected.

blocks.html: When Edwin Hubble first measured the law in 1929, he found about 500 km/s/Mpc, seven times today's value. His velocities were fine; his distances were too small, because the brightness of Cepheids was not yet calibrated correctly. It is a vivid example of how an error low on the distance ladder carries up into $H_0$, and of why every galaxy, not just ours, sees the same law: the expansion has no center.

Using $d = cz/H_0$ for large redshifts. It is a first-order approximation for $z \ll 1$. At $z = 1$, for example, it gives 4,300 Mpc, but the distance to such a galaxy depends on how the expansion rate changed while the light traveled, and "distance" itself must be defined carefully (now, then, or by brightness). Check: use the linear law only for $z$ below about 0.1.

blocks.html: Does the universe expand forever? The equation that answers it was found by Alexander Friedmann in 1922 from general relativity, but its heart can be derived with nothing more than orbital energy. It links the expansion rate to the density of the universe.

Picture a sphere of radius $R = ar$ cut out of a uniform universe of density $\rho$. By the shell theorem, a galaxy on its surface feels only the mass inside, $M = \tfrac43\pi R^3\rho$. Its energy per unit mass is constant: $$\tfrac12\dot R^2 - \frac{GM}{R} = \text{const}.$$ Divide by $\tfrac12R^2$ and use $H = \dot R/R = \dot a/a$: $$H^2 = \frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho - \frac{kc^2}{a^2},$$ where the constant has been written as $-kc^2/a^2$. General relativity gives the same equation and says what $k$ means: the curvature of space. The universe is flat ($k = 0$) when $\rho$ equals the critical density $\rho_c = 3H^2/(8\pi G)$.

The Friedmann equation $H^2 = \tfrac{8\pi G}{3}\rho - kc^2/a^2$. With $\Omega = \rho/\rho_c$: $\Omega > 1$ means positive curvature, $\Omega < 1$ negative, $\Omega = 1$ flat. Measurements (Planck satellite and others) find $\Omega$ equal to 1 within about 0.2%: about 31% matter and 69% dark energy.

blocks.name: ph-cosmic

opts.task: Change the amounts of matter and dark energy and watch how the expansion history changes.

blocks.cap: The scale factor over time for different mixes of matter and dark energy.

blocks.title: The critical density today
blocks.q: Find $\rho_c$ for $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc.
blocks.a: About $9.2 \times 10^{-27}$ kg/m³, the mass of about 5.5 hydrogen atoms per cubic meter.

blocks.title: The expansion rate in the past
blocks.q: With $\Omega_m = 0.31$ and $\Omega_\Lambda = 0.69$, $H(z) = H_0\sqrt{\Omega_m(1 + z)^3 + \Omega_\Lambda}$. Find $H$ at $z = 1$ for $H_0 = 70$.
blocks.a: About 125 km/s/Mpc: the universe expanded faster when it was denser.

blocks.title: Escape speed for the universe
blocks.q: For the sphere above, compare the expansion speed $v = HR$ with the escape speed $\sqrt{2GM/R}$.
steps: With matter alone, $\Omega < 1$ means faster than escape speed.
blocks.a: $v/v_{\text{esc}} = 1/\sqrt{\Omega}$: a matter-only universe with $\Omega < 1$ expands forever, and one with $\Omega > 1$ recollapses. Dark energy changes this story (next topic).

blocks.html: Thinking a "flat universe" is shaped like a pancake. Flat describes the geometry of space everywhere, in three dimensions: parallel lines stay parallel and the angles of a giant triangle add to 180°. A closed universe ($k > 0$) is like the surface of a sphere, with triangles adding to more than 180°; an open one like a saddle. None of them has an edge. Astronomers test it with triangles billions of light-years across, using the size of hot spots in the microwave background.

blocks.html: The Friedmann equation says the expansion rate is set by the density. But different ingredients dilute at different rates as the universe grows, so the mix changes over time, and each ingredient has its turn in charge.

Matter (ordinary and dark): the mass in a region stays fixed while its volume grows as $a^3$, so $\rho_m \propto a^{-3}$. Radiation (photons, and neutrinos early on): the number per volume also falls as $a^{-3}$, but each photon's wavelength stretches as $a$, so its energy falls as $a^{-1}$: $\rho_r \propto a^{-4}$. Dark energy, in the simplest model a cosmological constant, has the same density at every time: $\rho_\Lambda$ = const. Today $\Omega_r \approx 9 \times 10^{-5}$, $\Omega_m \approx 0.31$ and $\Omega_\Lambda \approx 0.69$. Going back in time ($a$ smaller, $z$ larger) radiation grows fastest, so it ruled the earliest era; then matter; and now dark energy.

$\rho_r \propto (1 + z)^4$, $\rho_m \propto (1 + z)^3$, $\rho_\Lambda$ constant. Radiation and matter were equal at $1 + z = \Omega_m/\Omega_r \approx 3400$ (about 50,000 years after the Big Bang); matter and dark energy were equal at $z \approx 0.3$, a few billion years ago. In the radiation era $a \propto t^{1/2}$, in the matter era $a \propto t^{2/3}$, and with dark energy in charge the expansion accelerates.

blocks.name: astrophys-plot
blocks.cap: The three densities against the scale factor on log–log axes: slopes $-4$, $-3$ and $0$. Where two lines cross, the two ingredients were equal; the highest line at any time is the one in charge. Drag the scale factor to compare them.

blocks.title: When did matter take over?
blocks.q: With $\Omega_m = 0.31$ and $\Omega_r = 9.0 \times 10^{-5}$, find the redshift of matter–radiation equality.
blocks.a: $z \approx 3400$.

blocks.title: When did dark energy take over?
blocks.q: With $\Omega_m = 0.31$ and $\Omega_\Lambda = 0.69$, find when the two densities were equal, and when the expansion began to speed up (when $\Omega_\Lambda = \tfrac12\Omega_m(1 + z)^3$).
blocks.a: The expansion started speeding up at $z \approx 0.65$, roughly 6 billion years ago; dark energy outweighed matter from $z \approx 0.3$.

blocks.title: Growth in the matter era
blocks.q: During the matter era, $a \propto t^{2/3}$. While the age of the universe grows by a factor of 8, how much do distances grow?
blocks.a: 4 times.

blocks.html: Thinking the mix of matter and radiation has always been what it is today. Radiation is now a tiny 0.009% of the total, but because its density grows as $(1 + z)^4$ going back, it outweighed matter before $z \approx 3400$. Dark energy, now 69%, was negligible in the early universe. Check: the ratio $\rho_r/\rho_m = (\Omega_r/\Omega_m)(1 + z)$ was about 0.3 even at $z = 1100$, when the microwave background was released.

blocks.html: Early on, the universe was filled with hot plasma, and light could not travel far before scattering off a free electron. About 380,000 years after the Big Bang it had cooled to about 3,000 K; electrons and nuclei combined into neutral atoms, and the universe became transparent. That light has traveled freely ever since. Stretched by the expansion (see redshift and the scale factor), it arrives today as the cosmic microwave background, with the spectrum of the Planck function.

Every photon's wavelength stretches by the same factor, $1 + z$. A Planck spectrum at temperature $T$ stays a Planck spectrum when every wavelength is multiplied by the same factor: it becomes a Planck spectrum at $T/(1 + z)$, since only the combination $\lambda T$ appears in $x = hc/(\lambda kT)$. So the background is still a nearly perfect blackbody, just cooler: $$T(z) = T_0(1 + z), \qquad T_0 = 2.725\text{ K}.$$ Why 3,000 K and not the 158,000 K that matches hydrogen's 13.6 eV? There are over a billion photons for every atom, and even at 3,000 K the rare photons in the Wien tail of the spectrum outnumbered the atoms enough to keep hydrogen ionized.

The CMB is a 2.725 K blackbody, peaking near 1.06 mm. It was released at $z \approx 1100$, when $T \approx 3000$ K. It fills all of space and arrives from every direction, the same to about one part in 100,000 once our own motion is accounted for.

blocks.name: ph-blackbody
blocks.cap: The background radiation as the universe expands: 3,000 K at release, then 300 K, 30 K and 2.725 K today. The shape stays a blackbody; it slides to longer wavelengths and lower intensity.

blocks.title: Where the CMB peaks today
blocks.q: Use Wien's law for $T = 2.725$ K.
blocks.a: $1.06 \times 10^{-3}$ m: about 1 mm, in the microwave band.

blocks.title: The redshift of release
blocks.q: When was the background at 3,000 K?
blocks.a: $z \approx 1100$. Its light then peaked near 970 nm, near-infrared, and the universe glowed like the surface of a red star.

blocks.title: Our motion through the background
blocks.q: The background looks hotter ahead of us and cooler behind, by $\Delta T \approx T(v/c)$. Our speed relative to it is 370 km/s. Find $\Delta T$.
blocks.a: About 3.4 mK. Removing this dipole reveals the tiny variations, about $10^{-5}$, that seeded galaxies.

blocks.html: Thinking the microwave background comes from one place in the sky, where the Big Bang happened. The Big Bang was not an explosion at a point in space; it happened everywhere, and the background was released everywhere at once. We see it coming from every direction because the light reaching us now left, from all around, at the time of release. Check: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found it in 1965 as a faint hiss their antenna picked up wherever they pointed it.

The COBE satellite (1990) measured its spectrum as a blackbody to better than one part in 10,000; the WMAP and Planck satellites mapped its tiny variations, which pin down the universe's age (13.8 billion years) and contents.

blocks.html: About a quarter of the ordinary matter in the universe is helium. Where did it come from? Stars make helium, as in the proton–proton chain, but not nearly enough. Most of it was made in the first few minutes, when the whole universe was as hot as a stellar core, a time we can reach by running the background radiation's temperature back.

Freeze-out. At first, weak reactions turned neutrons and protons into each other freely, keeping $n/p = e^{-\Delta mc^2/kT}$ with $\Delta mc^2 = 1.293$ MeV. About one second after the Big Bang, at $kT \approx 0.8$ MeV, these reactions became too slow to keep up, and the ratio froze near $e^{-1.293/0.8} \approx 1/5$ (a fuller calculation, which follows the reactions as they slow, gives about 1/6). Decay. Free neutrons decay (mean lifetime 879 s), so the ratio drifted down. The deuterium bottleneck. Deuterium is the first step to helium, but until the temperature fell to about $10^{9}$ K, energetic photons broke it apart as fast as it formed. About 3 to 4 minutes in, with $n/p$ down to about $1/7$, deuterium survived and nearly every neutron was swept into helium-4. With 2 neutrons and 2 protons per helium nucleus, the mass fraction is $$Y = \frac{2(n/p)}{1 + n/p} = \frac{2/7}{8/7} = 0.25.$$

Big Bang nucleosynthesis made about 25% helium by mass, plus traces of deuterium, helium-3 and lithium, in the first few minutes. The oldest gas has about 24 to 25% helium, and its deuterium matches the amount of ordinary matter measured from the microwave background. Stars have added only a few percent of helium since.

blocks.cap: After freeze-out, neutron decay lowers $n/p$. If nucleosynthesis had waited longer, there would be less helium. Starting from $1/5$, the ratio reaches about $1/7$ some 4 minutes later, giving $Y \approx 0.25$.

blocks.title: Helium from a neutron count
blocks.q: With 1 neutron for every 7 protons, what mass fraction ends up in helium-4?
steps: One helium-4 uses the 2 neutrons and 2 protons: 4 of 16 nucleons.

blocks.title: Freeze-out
blocks.q: Find $n/p$ at $kT = 0.8$ MeV.

blocks.title: Could stars have made the helium?
blocks.q: Suppose the Milky Way has shone at $2.5 \times 10^{10}\,L_\odot$ for 13 Gyr, all from turning hydrogen into helium ($0.0071c^2$ per kilogram). How much helium could that make, compared with its $6 \times 10^{10}\,M_\odot$ of stars and gas?
steps: Power: $2.5 \times 10^{10} \times 3.83 \times 10^{26} = 9.6 \times 10^{36}$ W. Time: $13 \times 10^{9} \times 3.16 \times 10^{7} = 4.1 \times 10^{17}$ s. Energy: $3.9 \times 10^{54}$ J.
blocks.a: About 5% of the mass, a rough estimate but far short of the 25% observed: most helium is primordial.

blocks.html: Thinking all of the helium in the universe was made in stars. Stars make helium, but even a whole galaxy shining for its entire life converts only a few percent of its mass. And helium is about 24% of the mass even in the oldest stars and the most pristine gas, which stars have hardly touched. Check with the estimate above: compare the energy a galaxy has radiated with the energy needed to make a quarter of its mass into helium.

The amounts of deuterium and helium-3 predicted by the theory match observations well. Lithium-7 is the exception: old stars show about three times less than predicted, a puzzle that is still being studied.
